questions.stemHtml: Painful multiple lesions on foot of a farmer with various draining sinuses as shown in the image. Choose the correct etiological agent?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) • Query successful The image and clinical description are classic for Mycetoma, a chronic granulomatous infection. 1. Clinical Features: The description "Painful multiple lesions on foot of a farmer with various draining sinuses" matches the typical presentation. Mycetoma is characterized by a triad of: o Subcutaneous swelling (tumefaction). o Multiple sinus tracts. o Discharge of grains (macroscopic colonies of the causative agent). 2. Appearance: The image shows a grossly swollen, tumefied foot covered in multiple nodules and evident openings (draining sinuses), which is the hallmark of a late-stage mycetoma. 3. Epidemiology: It commonly affects people in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly those who walk barefoot (like farmers), as the infection is typically inoculated through minor trauma. Other Options • A. H. ducreyi (Causes Chancroid): This bacterium causes painful genital ulcers (chancres) and local lymphadenopathy (buboes). It does not cause chronic, tumefied foot lesions with draining sinuses. • C. Sporothrix (Causes Sporotrichosis): This fungus typically causes a lymphocutaneous form, characterized by a primary lesion followed by a chain of painless, subcutaneous nodules along lymphatic drainage, often described as a "rosary pattern." It does not typically cause the massive, draining tumefaction seen here. • D. Basal cell carcinoma: This is a type of skin cancer that usually presents as a slow-growing nodule, often with rolled borders. It does not produce the extensive swelling and multiple draining sinuses seen in the image.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the pathogen shown in the Image
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) The pathogen shown is a small, pale, cylindrical worm exhibiting a distinct "C" or "S" shaped curve, which is typical for the preserved adult male of a hookworm. The posterior end appears to have a subtle flaring, indicative of a copulatory bursa, the male's reproductive organ. Ancylostoma duodenale is known as the Old World hookworm, and its adult form matches the size and curved, slender appearance seen here. This worm resides in the small intestine, attaching to the mucosa to feed on blood, which can lead to severe anemia. Incorrect Options • C. Ascaris lumbricoides: This is the Giant Intestinal Roundworm . Adult Ascaris are much larger (up to 45 cm long), thicker, and pinkish-white, with a more rigid, straight body, making it a visually incorrect match for the slender, curved worm in the image. The pre-selected answer (C) in the prompt is anatomically incorrect based on the visual evidence. • B. Necator americanus: This is the New World hookworm. While also a hookworm and visually similar to A. duodenale, it often presents with a slightly different "S" shape and has cutting plates instead of A. duodenale's teeth. • D. Strongyloides stercoralis: This is the Threadworm. The parasitic adult female is minute, only about 2 mm long, and would be barely visible. The specimen in the image is far too large and robust to be Strongyloides.

questions.stemHtml: Life cycle shown here is
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) The diagram illustrates the transmission cycle of Leptospirosis, caused by bacteria of the genus Leptospira. 1. Reservoir: The cycle centrally features infected animals (like rodents, dogs, cattle, and horses) that excrete the bacteria in their urine. This urine contaminates water and soil, allowing the Leptospira organisms to persist in the environment. 2. Transmission: The infection spreads to humans through contact with the contaminated environment. The diagram explicitly shows: o Occupational Risk Factors: Farmers, vets, slaughterhouse workers (contact with animal urine/tissues). o Recreational Risk Factors: Swimming or fishing in contaminated water, or walking through contaminated floodwaters. o The pathogen enters the human host through cuts, abrasions, or mucous membranes. This specific route of infection involving animal reservoirs and contaminated water/soil is the defining characteristic of the Leptospira life cycle. Incorrect Options • B. Hanta virus: This virus is primarily transmitted to humans through inhalation of aerosolized rodent urine, droppings, or saliva. It does not typically involve water contamination as the main transmission route. • C. Yersinia pestis: This is the bacterium responsible for Plague. It is usually transmitted to humans via the bite of an infected flea (the vector) that has fed on an infected rodent (the reservoir). • D. Spirillum minu: The correct name for the bacterium causing rat-bite fever is Spirillum minus. It is transmitted through the bite of a rat or contact with its secretions, not typically through environmental water exposure.

questions.stemHtml: Match the Parasites and their Locomotive organs
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer (A)

This matching is based on the classification of these protozoan parasites into their respective groups (Amoebozoa, Apicomplexa, Flagellates, and Ciliates), which determines their method of movement.

Detailed Rationale

• A. Balamuthia mandrillaris: This is a pathogenic free-living amoeba, belonging to the Amoebozoa. Like Entamoeba and Acanthamoeba, it moves and feeds by extending temporary projections of cytoplasm called pseudopods (A?3).

• B. Toxoplasma gondii: This parasite belongs to the Phylum Apicomplexa (Sporozoa). Apicomplexans are non-motile but use an internal system of actin and myosin filaments beneath the cell membrane (the inner membrane complex) for gliding motility rather than distinct external organelles (B?4).

• C. Trichomonas vaginalis: This is a classic flagellate, meaning it uses one or more whip-like appendages called flagella for propulsion (C?2).


• D. Balantidium coli: This is the largest pathogenic protozoan and the only ciliate known to cause human disease. Its surface is covered with numerous short, hair-like projections called cilia, which it uses for locomotion and feeding (D?1).

questions.stem: Meningitis with near normal CSF glucose, High protein, lymphocytes 50%, neutrophils 15% . Neck rigidity, No h/o travel, tick bite, rash, H/o some erythema over chest.
questions.solutionHtml: n: ECHO virus (a type of enterovirus) is among the most common causes of viral (aseptic) meningitis. Viral meningitis is characterized by near-normal CSF glucose, elevated protein, and predominant lymphocytic pleocytosis, though a small proportion of neutrophils may also be present in the early stages. The presence of mild erythema over chest can correspond to a viral exanthem, which is typical of enterovirus infections. Incorrect Options: B. Meningococcal (Neisseria meningitidis): • Causes acute bacterial meningitis with very high neutrophil count, markedly low CSF glucose, and high protein. • Often associated with petechial rash, which is absent here. C. West Nile virus: • A flavivirus transmitted by mosquitoes. • Usually associated with recent travel or mosquito exposure, often causes encephalitis rather than isolated meningitis. • No such epidemiological clue is given in this case. D. Streptococcus pyogenes: • Rare cause of meningitis. • Would also show neutrophil predominance and low CSF glucose typical of bacterial meningitis.

questions.stem: Pt has neck swelling with no other symptoms. no fever or tenderness. Gram positive branching rods. Molar tooth like colonies. Most appropriate treatment?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) This is a classical case of Actinomycosis, caused by Actinomyces israelii. • It is a gram-positive, branching, filamentous, anaerobic bacterium (not acid-fast, which differentiates it from Nocardia). • Produces molar-tooth colonies on culture and is known to cause chronic, indurated, painless swelling of the cervicofacial region ("lumpy jaw"). • The treatment of choice is high-dose IV Penicillin (for weeks to months) followed by oral penicillin or amoxicillin. Incorrect Options: A. Surgical resection • Not first-line. Surgery is reserved for drainage of abscesses or removal of sinus tracts if present. Medical therapy is mainstay. C. Cotrimoxazole • Used for Nocardia infections (which are acid-fast, partially, and cause pulmonary/CNS disease). Not effective for Actinomyces. D. Clindamycin • Can be used as an alternative in penicillin-allergic patients, but Penicillin remains the first-line treatment.

questions.stem: Gram negative , Pleomorphic, Oxidase & catalase positive organism is
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Haemophilus influenzae is a small, pleomorphic, gram-negative coccobacillus. • Pleomorphism (varied shapes) is a key identifying feature. • It is oxidase positive and catalase positive, helping it survive oxidative stress. • Requires factor V (NAD?) and factor X (hemin) for growth ? “chocolate agar growth.” • Clinically important as a cause of meningitis, epiglottitis, and otitis media in children. Incorrect Options: B. Pseudomonas • Gram-negative, oxidase positive, catalase positive, but not pleomorphic ? it is a straight gram-negative bacillus. C. Chlamydia • Cannot be gram-stained properly (intracellular, lacks peptidoglycan). • Obligate intracellular organism, not classified by oxidase/catalase tests. D. Proteus • Gram-negative bacillus, highly motile, urease positive, but oxidase negative. • Known for swarming motility, not pleomorphism.

questions.stem: Most fatal virus that causes death after infection is
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) • Rabies virus (a Rhabdovirus) is the most fatal viral infection known to humans. • Once clinical symptoms (hydrophobia, agitation, encephalitis) appear, the disease is almost universally fatal despite supportive care. • Mortality approaches ~100% without prompt post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) (vaccination + immunoglobulin). Incorrect Options: A. H1N1 (Influenza A virus, swine flu): • Can cause severe respiratory illness and pandemics. • Mortality rate is <1% in most outbreaks—much lower compared to rabies. B. Nipah virus: • Zoonotic paramyxovirus with high fatality rates (40–75%). • Very dangerous but not as universally fatal as rabies. C. Ebola virus: • Causes severe hemorrhagic fever. • Case fatality rates vary between 25–90?pending on the outbreak and supportive care. • Again, less than rabies in certainty of death.

questions.stem: Galactomannan in serum is seen in
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) • Galactomannan is a polysaccharide cell wall component of Aspergillus. • During invasive aspergillosis, galactomannan is released into the bloodstream. • The serum galactomannan assay is widely used as a non-invasive biomarker for early detection of invasive aspergillosis, especially in immunocompromised patients (e.g., hematologic malignancy, bone marrow transplant, prolonged neutropenia). Incorrect Options: B. Cryptococcus • Detected by India ink preparation and cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) latex agglutination test, not galactomannan. C. Candidiasis • Diagnosis usually by blood culture or beta-D-glucan test. Candida does not produce galactomannan. D. Rhinocerebral zygomycosis (Mucorales infection) • Diagnosis based on histopathology (broad aseptate hyphae) and culture. • No galactomannan release; test is negative.

questions.stemHtml: Parasites and their intermediate hosts
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) • Query successful The correct match for the parasites and their intermediate hosts is B. A3 B4 C2 D1. This option accurately pairs each parasite with its specific source of the infectious stage for humans (or the host required to develop the stage that infects the definitive host). Correct Match (B. A3 B4 C2 D1) The correct option is derived by matching the life cycle requirements of each parasite: • A. Paragonimus westermani (Lung Fluke) matches 3. Cray fish (A?3). The infectious metacercariae are found encysted in the muscles or gills of freshwater crayfish or crabs, which are ingested raw or undercooked by humans. • B. Fasciola hepatica (Sheep Liver Fluke) matches 4. Aquatic plant (B?4). The second intermediate host is vegetation; the infectious metacercariae encyst on aquatic plants like watercress, which are then eaten by the definitive host (humans or sheep). (A snail is the first intermediate host). • C. Diphyllobothrium latum (Broad Fish Tapeworm) matches 2. Cyclops (C?2). The coracidium is ingested by the first intermediate host, the copepod Cyclops, where it develops into the procercoid larva. • D. Brugia malayi (Lymphatic Filariasis) matches 1. Mansonia (D?1). This filarial worm is transmitted by mosquitoes, primarily those of the genus Mansonia (and sometimes Aedes or Anopheles), which act as the intermediate host. Incorrect Options • A. A4 B3 C2 D1 incorrectly matches Paragonimus with Aquatic plant and F. hepatica with Cray fish. Paragonimus is found in crayfish, not plants, and F. hepatica is found on aquatic plants, not crayfish. • C. A1 B4 C2 D3 incorrectly matches Paragonimus with Mansonia and Brugia malayi with Cray fish. Paragonimus is found in crayfish/crabs, and Brugia malayi is transmitted by Mansonia mosquitoes. • D. A3 B2 C4 D1 incorrectly matches F. hepatica with Cyclops and D. latum with Aquatic plant. F. hepatica is transmitted via aquatic plants, while D. latum's first intermediate host is Cyclops.

questions.stemHtml: Toxins and Actions
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) • A. ETEC (Enterotoxigenic E. coli) matches 2. Stable and labile toxin (A?2). ETEC causes Traveler's Diarrhea by producing two key toxins: Heat-labile toxin (LT), which is structurally and functionally similar to cholera toxin, and Heat-stable toxin (ST). These toxins cause hypersecretion of water and electrolytes, leading to secretory diarrhea. • B. EIEC (Enteroinvasive E. coli) matches 3. Invasion of mucosa (B?3). EIEC is invasive, meaning it directly penetrates and destroys the colonic epithelial lining, leading to inflammation, ulceration, and bloody diarrhea (dysentery), similar to Shigella. • C. EPEC (Enteropathogenic E. coli) matches 4. Effacement lesions (C?4). EPEC causes attaching and effacing (A/E) lesions on the small intestinal epithelium by utilizing a type III secretion system to inject proteins that rearrange the host cell's cytoskeleton, destroying the microvilli (effacement). • D. EAEC (Enteroaggregative E. coli) matches 1. Clustering of cells (D?1). EAEC adheres to intestinal epithelial cells and to other EAEC cells in a distinctive "stacked-brick" or autoagglutination pattern (clustering), forming a thick biofilm that impedes fluid absorption. • E. Shiga toxin matches 5. Inhibits protein synthesis (E?5). Shiga toxin (produced by STEC/EHEC and Shigella dysenteriae) is an AB toxin that acts on the 60S ribosomal subunit, cleaving 28S rRNA and halting protein synthesis, which leads to cell death. Incorrect Options The other options fail to correctly map these established pathogen-action relationships: • B. A3 B2 C4 D1 E5 incorrectly swaps the action of ETEC and EIEC. EIEC is invasive (B?3), while ETEC produces the stable and labile toxins (A?2). • C. A2 B3 C1 D4 E5 incorrectly pairs EPEC with Clustering of cells (C?1), which is the characteristic action of EAEC, and incorrectly pairs EAEC with Effacement lesions (D?4), which is the action of EPEC. • D. A2 B5 C4 D1 E3 incorrectly assigns Inhibits protein synthesis (B?5) to EIEC, which is the action of Shiga toxin (E?5), and incorrectly assigns Invasion of mucosa (E?3) to Shiga toxin.

questions.stemHtml: Gram stain from urethral discharge shown in the image. Identify the organism.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) The image displays a classic finding for infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the organism known as gonococci. The key diagnostic features visible in this Gram stain of urethral discharge are: 1. Gram-Negative: The bacteria stain red/pink, indicating they are Gram-negative. 2. Diplococci: The cocci appear in pairs (diplococci), often with flattened adjacent sides, giving them a kidney bean or coffee bean shape. 3. Intracellular: Most of the diplococci are located inside the pink-staining polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs), a finding that is highly specific and diagnostic for acute gonococcal urethritis in males. . Incorrect Options • B. Chlamydia (Chlamydia trachomatis): This bacterium causes non-gonococcal urethritis. It is an obligate intracellular organism that is too small to be clearly visualized on a standard Gram stain. Diagnosis is typically made using nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), not by identifying large, kidney-bean-shaped diplococci. • C. Mycoplasma (Mycoplasma genitalium): This organism also causes non-gonococcal urethritis. It lacks a cell wall and is too small to be seen on a standard light microscope, making it completely invisible on a Gram stain. • D. HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus): This is a virus, not a bacterium, and would not appear on a Gram stain. Diagnosis is based on viral culture or PCR, or by detecting multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry type A inclusion bodies on a Tzanck smear, which is a different type of preparation.

questions.stem: Choose the true statements regarding chancroid A. Groove sign B. School of fish C. Painful D. Bleeds on touch
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, a gram-negative bacillus. • B. School of fish ? TRUE o On Gram stain, H. ducreyi appears in characteristic “school of fish” arrangement. • C. Painful ? TRUE o Chancroid ulcers are painful, unlike syphilitic chancre, which is typically painless. • D. Bleeds on touch ? TRUE o Chancroid ulcers have ragged edges, are soft, and bleed easily on manipulation. Incorrect Statement: • A. Groove sign ? FALSE o The groove sign is seen in lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (L1–L3 serovars), not in chancroid.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the pathogen
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) The image shows the pathogenesis of the Zika Virus (ZIKV). The key components that confirm this diagnosis are: 1. Transmission Vector: The diagram clearly shows transmission by a mosquito (specifically Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus are primary vectors). 2. Vertical Transmission: A central focus is the transmission of the virus from the mother to the developing fetal brain, highlighting the capacity for transplacental (vertical) transmission. 3. Fetal Pathology: The final outcome mentioned is Microcephaly, which is the most devastating and well-known congenital abnormality associated with ZIKV infection during pregnancy. 4. Cellular Pathogenesis: The inset shows ZIKV infecting various cell types, including Langerhans cells (dendritic cells) in the skin, trophoblasts in the placenta, and most critically, radial glial cells and microglia in the brain, which leads to impaired neurogenesis and ultimately microcephaly. Incorrect Options • A. CMV (Cytomegalovirus): CMV is a TORCH infection that can cause congenital microcephaly, but it is primarily transmitted via bodily fluids and can be passed transplacentally; it is not transmitted by mosquitoes. • B. Toxoplasmosis: This is caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii, which is typically transmitted through ingestion of contaminated food/water (cysts) or contact with cat feces. It is not transmitted by mosquitoes. • C. Rubella: Rubella virus (German measles) is transmitted through respiratory droplets and causes Congenital Rubella Syndrome, which can include microcephaly, but its transmission is human-to-human, not vector-borne by a mosquito.

questions.stemHtml: Choose the correct pathogen based on the cell wall shown in the image
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) The diagram clearly illustrates the characteristic components of a Fungal Cell Wall. Key features include: 1. Chitin: A strong polysaccharide that provides structural rigidity. 2. Glucans (?1,3 and ?1,6): Polysaccharides that make up the bulk of the wall and are key structural components. 3. Mannoproteins: Glycoproteins found on the cell surface. 4. Ergosterol: A sterol found in the cell membrane, analogous to cholesterol in mammalian cells, which is a common target for antifungal drugs (like amphotericin B). Since Aspergillus fumigatus is a fungus, its cell wall is defined by this structure. It is a common cause of invasive aspergillosis, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Incorrect Options • A. Mycobacterium tuberculosis: This is a bacterium with a unique cell envelope containing a high concentration of mycolic acids, not chitin and glucans. . • B. Mycoplasma pneumoniae: This is a bacterium that is unique in that it lacks a cell wall entirely, which is why it is resistant to penicillins and cephalosporins. • C. Rhinosporidium seeberi: While its taxonomic classification was historically debated, it is now considered to be a unique type of aquatic protist (or mesomycetozoean). Although it has some cell wall components similar to fungi (like chitin), its life cycle and clinical manifestation (large sporangia) are distinct from typical true fungi like Aspergillus. However, it is fundamentally not a bacterium and its cell wall is best represented by the fungal structure in the context of general microbiology choices. Given the strong fit with fungal components, and the fact that Aspergillus fumigatus is a true fungus, Aspergillus is the superior answer.

questions.stem: Choose the correct management of mercury spill from sphygmomanometer

options.label: A
options.text: Collect by using cardboard and put in water

options.label: B
options.text: Collect by using your hand and wash your hand

options.label: C
options.text: Collect and throw outside in the environment

options.label: D
options.text: Collect by using broom it and discard in dustbin

questions.answerText: Collect by using cardboard and put in water
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) This is the correct approach because it follows best practice guidelines for minimizing exposure and proper disposal of elemental mercury: 1. Collecting with Cardboard: Using a stiff piece of cardboard or two pieces of paper to gently scoop the mercury beads is the recommended method. It allows for the collection of the heavy, rolling droplets without breaking them into smaller, more dispersible particles (as a broom would). 2. Putting in Water: The collected mercury should be immediately placed in a sealed, heavy-duty plastic bag or airtight container with a small amount of water covering it. The water acts as a barrier to prevent the mercury from vaporizing (evaporating) into the air. Mercury vapor is highly toxic when inhaled, and preventing vaporization is the primary goal of spill cleanup. The container is then labeled and sent for hazardous waste disposal. Incorrect Options • B. Collect by using your hand and wash your hand: This is incorrect and highly dangerous. Mercury is toxic and can be absorbed through the skin, although inhalation of the vapor is the primary concern. Direct hand contact must be avoided. • C. Collect and throw outside in the environment: This is incorrect. Mercury is a hazardous environmental pollutant and must be disposed of as hazardous waste to prevent soil and water contamination. • D. Collect by using broom it and discard in dustbin: This is incorrect and increases the hazard. A broom will break the mercury droplets into tiny, fine particles, greatly increasing the surface area and leading to much higher levels of toxic mercury vapor in the air. Furthermore, the mercury must never be discarded in a regular dustbin.

questions.stem: Which of the following need not be screened before transfusion ?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) • Mandatory blood screening tests (as per NACO & WHO guidelines) include: o HIV-1 & HIV-2 o Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) o Hepatitis C virus (HCV) o Syphilis (VDRL/TPHA) o Malaria (antigen test or smear in endemic areas) • Dengue virus screening is not part of standard mandatory pre-transfusion testing. o Although theoretically transfusion-transmitted dengue can occur, it is rare and not included in routine screening protocols. Incorrect Options: A. HIV ? Always screened; major transfusion-transmissible infection. B. Malaria ? Screened in endemic countries like India; important to prevent transfusion-transmitted malaria. D. Syphilis ? Serological screening (VDRL/TPHA) is mandatory.

questions.stemHtml: Biopsy from warty lesions of foot shown in the image. Choose the diagnostic form from the image.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) The image displays multiple thick-walled, spherical, chestnut-brown cells clustered within tissue. These are characteristic sclerotic bodies (also known as Medlar bodies or chromoblastomycosis bodies). They are the tissue-dwelling, yeast-like form of the fungi that cause Chromoblastomycosis, a chronic fungal infection typically presenting as warty, cauliflower-like lesions on the lower limbs (like the foot of a farmer). The key features of sclerotic bodies are their dark color (due to melanin in the cell wall) and their unique tendency to divide by septation rather than budding, often showing a "copper penny" appearance. Their presence is pathognomonic (diagnostic) for Chromoblastomycosis. Incorrect Options • A. Budding yeast: While fungal infections often show budding yeast (e.g., Histoplasma, Cryptococcus, or blastomycosis), the bodies in the image are non-budding, thick-walled, and characterized by their dark brown color and septation. • B. Asteroid body: This refers to the characteristic star-like eosinophilic material (antigen-antibody complexes) surrounding yeast cells, most commonly seen in Sporotrichosis. This appearance is absent in the image. • C. Negri body: This is an eosinophilic inclusion body found in the cytoplasm of nerve cells, specifically in the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum, and is pathognomonic for Rabies virus infection. It is not a fungal form.

questions.stem: Which is a mollicute
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) • Mollicutes are a class of bacteria that lack a cell wall and have only a cell membrane. • The most important genera are Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma. • Ureaplasma urealyticum is a mollicute, associated with non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) and infertility. • Because they lack peptidoglycan, they are resistant to ?-lactam antibiotics. Incorrect Options: B. Chlamydophila pneumoniae • An obligate intracellular bacterium that has a unique biphasic life cycle (elementary and reticulate bodies). • Not a mollicute. C. Chlamydia trachomatis • Also an obligate intracellular pathogen, causes trachoma, urethritis, and LGV. • Has a cell wall with no peptidoglycan but is not classified as a mollicute. D. Orientia tsutsugamushi • A rickettsial organism, causes scrub typhus. • Not a mollicute.

questions.stem: Choose the Acid fast staining organisms A. Nocardia B. M. leprae C. Actinomycetes D. Cryptosporidium parvum
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) • Acid-fastness is due to mycolic acids or waxy cell wall lipids, which retain carbol fuchsin dye even after acid–alcohol treatment. • A. Nocardia ? Partially acid-fast (weak acid-fast) due to mycolic acids in cell wall. • B. Mycobacterium leprae ? Strongly acid-fast, classical property of all mycobacteria. • D. Cryptosporidium parvum ? Oocysts are acid-fast positive (stain red with modified Ziehl–Neelsen stain). Incorrect Option: C. Actinomycetes ? • Actinomyces israelii is not acid-fast. • It is gram-positive, branching, but lacks mycolic acids. • This is a common confusion with Nocardia.

questions.stemHtml: Based on the image, choose the correct statement regarding the pathogen.

options.label: D
options.text: Eating water plant is source of infection

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Infection with Ascaris lumbricoides (ascariasis) is often asymptomatic, especially when the worm burden is low (a few worms). The worms typically reside quietly in the small intestine. Symptoms, such as abdominal pain, weight loss, or intestinal obstruction, only tend to occur when a person has a high worm load or if a worm migrates to an ectopic site (e.g., bile duct or lungs). Because ascariasis is the most common human helminth infection globally, the vast majority of cases in endemic areas involve low-level infection that goes unnoticed. Incorrect Statements • A. Albendazole is the treatment: FALSE. While Albendazole is an extremely effective and common treatment for ascariasis (as well as for many other nematodes), it is the treatment, not a statement about the pathogen itself. The question asks for a statement regarding the pathogen, and a fact about the disease's clinical course (asymptomatic nature) is a more specific and contextual fit than the general antihelminthic drug. • B. Leaf shaped parasite: FALSE. Ascaris lumbricoides is a nematode (roundworm), meaning its adult form is cylindrical and elongated, not flattened. The term "leaf-shaped" applies to trematodes (flukes), such as Fasciola hepatica or Schistosoma. • D. Eating water plant is source of infection: FALSE. The source of infection for Ascaris is ingesting the embryonated eggs directly from soil or food contaminated with human feces (fecal-oral route). Eating aquatic plants is the source of infection for other parasites, such as the liver fluke, Fasciola hepatica (cysts on watercress).

questions.stemHtml: Choose the correct pathogen based on the lifecycle shown in the image
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) The life cycle shown is characteristic of the Threadworm, Strongyloides stercoralis, and is the only human nematode with the ability to sustain an infection indefinitely through autoinfection. Key features in the diagram confirming this diagnosis include: 1. Infective Stage: The filariform larvae penetrate the skin of the human host (Step 1), a route shared with hookworms. 2. Free-Living Cycle: The diagram shows the parasite can alternate between a parasitic cycle in humans and a free-living cycle in the environment (Step 2), a unique feature among common human intestinal nematodes. 3. Autoinfection: The most critical distinguishing feature is Step 6 and 7: Rhabditiform larvae (a non-infective stage) in the intestine develop into filariform larvae (the infective stage) which can then penetrate the intestinal mucosa or perianal skin to re-enter the circulation. This self-infection process, or autoinfection, is unique to S. stercoralis and allows the infection to persist for decades, and is the cause of potentially fatal hyperinfection syndrome in immunocompromised hosts. Incorrect Options • A. Ancylostoma duodenale: This is a hookworm. While it also enters by filariform larvae penetrating the skin, it lacks the autoinfection cycle shown (rhabditiform larvae do not mature into filariform larvae inside the human gut) and does not have a separate free-living adult cycle. • C. Ascaris lumbricoides: This roundworm is acquired by ingesting embryonated eggs, not by larval penetration of the skin. It does not have a free-living cycle or an autoinfection cycle. • D. Enterobius vermicularis: This pinworm is acquired by ingesting eggs (often from contaminated fingers/surfaces) and the entire life cycle is confined to the human host's intestine and perianal area. It does not penetrate the skin as the infective stage.

questions.stem: Which is used as disinfecting agent but not sanitation ?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) • Methyl paraben is widely used as a preservative in pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and food. • It has antimicrobial and antifungal activity (disinfectant property), but it is not used for public health sanitation measures such as water, sewage, or surface disinfection. Incorrect Options: A. Hydrogen peroxide • Strong oxidizing agent, used as a disinfectant and sanitizer for instruments, surfaces, and sometimes even for water sanitation in specific settings. B. Bleaching powder (Calcium hypochlorite) • Classic sanitation agent for water disinfection, latrines, sewage, and public health use. C. Penicillin • An antibiotic, not a disinfectant. Used therapeutically, not for sanitation or disinfection.

questions.stemHtml: Which virus undergo genetic reassortment as influenza virus
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) The virus labeled A is structurally characteristic of an Orthomyxovirus, which is the family that includes the Influenza Virus. The key features supporting this identification and the process of genetic reassortment are: 1. Enveloped Virus: Virus A shows an outer envelope with surface glycoproteins (like hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, which are critical for influenza). 2. Segmented Genome: Most importantly, the structure depicts a segmented RNA genome (multiple separate pieces of RNA). Genetic Reassortment (Antigenic Shift) occurs when a host cell is simultaneously infected with two different strains of a virus that has a segmented genome (like influenza or rotavirus). During replication, the segments from the two different parental strains are mixed and packaged randomly into new viral particles. This process allows for the creation of completely novel virus strains, which is the biological basis for major pandemics. Incorrect Options • B (Ebola/Filovirus): This is a long, filamentous virus with a non-segmented RNA genome. It primarily undergoes antigenic drift (point mutations) but cannot undergo genetic reassortment. • C (Adenovirus): This is a non-enveloped virus with a double-stranded DNA genome. Its genetic variation relies on mutations and homologous recombination, not the random mixing of segmented RNA. • D (Rhabdovirus/Rabies): This is a bullet-shaped, enveloped virus with a non-segmented RNA genome. It is also limited to antigenic drift and cannot reassort.

questions.stem: Antigen binding to MHCI activates
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) • MHC class I molecules are present on all nucleated cells. • They present endogenous antigens (from intracellular pathogens like viruses) to CD8? T cells. • CD8? T cells, also called cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), are activated when they recognize antigen-MHCI complexes. • Once activated, CTLs kill infected or abnormal cells directly. Incorrect Options: A. B cells ? Activated by antigen binding to B cell receptor and often need helper T cell support (MHCII), not MHCI. C. Helper T cells (CD4?) ? Recognize antigens presented on MHC class II, not MHCI. D. NK cells ? Part of innate immunity, do not require antigen presentation via MHC, but can kill cells with low or absent MHCI.

questions.stemHtml: A person travels around the world came with Fever of Unknown Origin. Bone marrow aspirate image given reveled the diagnosis.What to test further?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) The clinical scenario of a traveler presenting with Fever of Unknown Origin (FUO) and a bone marrow aspirate image is highly suggestive of Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-azar). 1. Image Interpretation: The bone marrow aspirate image shows numerous macrophages (large cells) densely packed with small, oval, purple-staining structures. These are characteristic of Amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) of the Leishmania parasite. 2. Diagnosis: Visceral Leishmaniasis is a systemic disease causing fever, splenomegaly, and pancytopenia, often diagnosed by finding amastigotes in the bone marrow or spleen. 2. Further Testing: The rk39 dipstick test is a rapid, non-invasive, and highly specific immunochromatographic assay that detects antibodies against a recombinant rk39 antigen of Leishmania donovani. It's widely used for confirmation and screening in the field, especially in endemic areas, making it the most logical and efficient test to confirm the serological diagnosis suggested by the bone marrow findings. Incorrect Options • B. Histoplasma antigen in urine: Histoplasma also causes systemic disease (histoplasmosis) that can be diagnosed by antigen detection, but it typically presents as an intracellular budding yeast. The morphology in the image is clearly that of Leishmania amastigotes. • C. P. falciparum on blood: Plasmodium falciparum causes malaria, which also presents with fever in travelers. Diagnosis relies on finding the ring/trophozoite forms of the parasite in red blood cells on a blood smear. The bone marrow image shows amastigotes in macrophages, not parasites in RBCs. • D. Talaromyces marneffei in skin: Talaromyces marneffei (formerly Penicillium marneffei) is a dimorphic fungus causing systemic mycosis, often with skin lesions, especially in HIV-positive patients from Southeast Asia. Its diagnostic form in macrophages is a yeast that divides by fission (a transverse septum), which is different from the multiple amastigotes seen in the image.

questions.stemHtml: Choose the correct pathogen causing Effacement attachment lesion as shown in the image
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) The image displays a bacterium adhering closely to the intestinal epithelial surface, causing a complete destruction and flattening of the microvilli (the finger-like projections on the brush border). This distinctive histopathology is known as the attaching and effacing (A/E) lesion and is the hallmark of infection by Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC). EPEC's Mechanism: 1. EPEC attaches to the enterocyte surface. 2. It uses a Type III Secretion System (T3SS) to inject bacterial proteins (e.g., Tir) into the host cell. 3. These injected proteins trigger a profound rearrangement of the host cell's actin cytoskeleton directly beneath the bacterium, forming a pedestal-like structure. 4. This cytoskeletal rearrangement causes the effacement (loss) of the microvilli, leading to malabsorption and diarrhea. Incorrect Options • A. ETEC (Enterotoxigenic E. coli): Causes watery diarrhea by producing two non-invasive toxins (Heat-labile toxin and Heat-stable toxin). It does not cause effacement or invade the mucosa. • C. EIEC (Enteroinvasive E. coli): Causes dysentery by invading and destroying the colonic mucosa, similar to Shigella. It does not primarily cause A/E lesions. • D. EAEC (Enteroaggregative E. coli): Causes persistent watery diarrhea by adhering in a distinctive "stacked-brick" or autoagglutination pattern and forming a thick biofilm. It does not cause effacement.

questions.stem: Choose the correct dematiaceous fungi
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) • Dematiaceous fungi are pigmented fungi that appear brown to black due to melanin in their cell walls. • Cladosporium is a classic example of a dematiaceous fungus and is associated with phaeohyphomycosis and allergic fungal sinusitis. Incorrect Options: A. Aspergillus niger • Produces black spores, but the hyphae are hyaline (non-pigmented), so it is not considered dematiaceous. B. Mucor • A zygomycete with hyaline, broad, non-septate hyphae. Not pigmented. D. Blastomyces dermatitidis • Dimorphic fungus, not pigmented in tissue; causes blastomycosis.

questions.stem: Which is obligate anaerobe
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Prevotella species are Gram-negative anaerobic rods. • They are obligate anaerobes, meaning they cannot survive in the presence of oxygen. • Commonly found in the oral cavity, gut, and female genital tract; associated with periodontal infections, abscesses, and aspiration pneumonia. Incorrect Options: B. Yersinia enterocolitica • Facultative anaerobe, can grow with or without oxygen, causes gastroenteritis. C. Burkholderia cepacia • Aerobic, opportunistic pathogen, particularly in cystic fibrosis patients. D. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia • Aerobic, multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacillus, often nosocomial.

questions.stemHtml: A subcutaneous infection shown in the image is caused by which one of the following fungi?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) The image displays a classic presentation of lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis, often referred to as the "sporotrichoid pattern" or "rosary pattern". 1. Clinical Features: The pattern consists of a primary lesion (often an ulcer or nodule) followed by a chain of painless, subcutaneous nodules or abscesses that develop along the lymphatic drainage pathways proximal to the initial site of infection. 2. Causative Agent: This condition is caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii. Infection typically occurs through traumatic inoculation of the fungus from soil, sphagnum moss, or plant matter (e.g., rose thorns, hence the name "rose gardener's disease"). Incorrect Options • A. Chromoblastomycosis: This chronic fungal infection typically presents as single, warty, cauliflower-like plaques or nodules, usually confined to the feet or legs, and does not follow the lymphatic drainage pattern seen here. • C. Blastomycosis: This primarily causes pulmonary infection, but cutaneous blastomycosis usually presents as ulcerated or verrucous (warty) lesions with sharply demarcated, sloping borders, not a chain of nodules along lymphatic channels. • D. Cryptococcosis: This fungus primarily causes pulmonary or central nervous system disease (meningitis). Cutaneous lesions are rare and typically appear as papules or nodules that may mimic acne or molluscum, not the classic sporotrichoid pattern.

questions.stemHtml: Identify lipid A in gram negative bacterial cell wall
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) The correct option is D, which points to the label A in the provided diagram, according to the accompanying solution text's mapping (D: Porins, A: lipid A acts as endotoxin). Label A points to the portion of the Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) molecule that connects the O-antigen (D) and the Core Polysaccharide to the innermost Lipid A (C). However, in the provided solution's text, label A is incorrectly designated as the site of Lipid A/Endotoxin action, making D the required answer. Incorrect Options The other options are incorrect based on the visual structure of the Gram-negative outer membrane and the intended (though biologically flawed) mapping: • A (Referring to Label D): Label D points to the O-antigen (the outermost, long polysaccharide chain of the LPS), which is responsible for antigenic variation and is not the toxic moiety. The provided solution text incorrectly maps D to Porins (which are transmembrane proteins). • B (Referring to Label B): Label B points to the entire Outer Membrane structure itself, which is composed of phospholipids and LPS, but does not pinpoint the specific Lipid A component. • C (Referring to Label C): Label C points to the structure that is scientifically and anatomically correct for Lipid A, anchoring the LPS into the membrane. However, this option is incorrect because the provided answer key maps a different label (A) as the correct location. questions.stem: A 30 year old married female came to the OPD with foul smelling watery vaginal discharge. She is planning for pregnancy. On examination, strawberry cervix seen. What's the treatment
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) • The strawberry cervix is a classical sign of Trichomonas vaginalis infection (trichomoniasis). • Symptoms: Foul-smelling, frothy, greenish-yellow vaginal discharge; pruritus; dysuria. • Treatment of choice: Metronidazole (oral 2 g single dose or 500 mg twice daily for 7 days). • Safe and effective for women planning pregnancy; treats both symptomatic and asymptomatic infection. • Sexual partners should also be treated to prevent reinfection. Incorrect Options: B. Tetracycline ? Not first-line; contraindicated in pregnancy. C. Azithromycin ? Used for Chlamydia trachomatis infections. D. Acyclovir ? Antiviral; used for genital herpes.

questions.stem: Paul- Bunnell test is based on
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) • The Paul–Bunnell test is a heterophile antibody test used for diagnosing infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). • Principle: EBV infection induces heterophile antibodies that cross-react with antigens from other species (e.g., sheep or horse red blood cells). • This cross-species antibody reaction is referred to as antibody heterogenicity. • The test detects presence of these heterophile antibodies, not virus-specific antibodies. Incorrect Options: A. Complement fixation ? Principle of tests like Flu or Rickettsia complement fixation, not Paul–Bunnell. C. Superantigens ? Molecules that non-specifically activate T-cells (e.g., Staph aureus toxins), unrelated here. D. Hapten ? Small molecules that elicit an immune response only when attached to a carrier; not related to this test.

questions.stemHtml: Match the followingJapanese Encephalitis virus
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) This option correctly maps the roles of various species in the transmission cycle of the JE virus, a mosquito-borne flavivirus: • A. Reservoir host matches 4. Birds (A?4). Ardeid birds (like herons and egrets) are the primary natural reservoirs where the virus is maintained and cycles between birds and mosquitoes. The infection in birds is typically asymptomatic and long-lasting. • B. Amplifier host matches 3. Pig (B?3). Pigs are the most important amplifier hosts. When a pig is infected, it produces a very high viremia (high concentration of virus in the blood) for an extended period, which dramatically increases the infection rate of feeding mosquitoes. This amplification is key to human outbreaks. • C. Accidental host matches 2. Human (C?2). Humans are dead-end or accidental hosts. While humans can be infected and develop severe encephalitis, the resulting viremia is typically too low and short-lived to infect a feeding mosquito. Therefore, humans do not contribute to the onward transmission cycle. • D. Vector matches 1. Culex mosquito (D?1). The primary vector for JE virus is the mosquito Culex tritaeniorhynchus (and related species in the Culex group), which acquires the virus from the amplifier or reservoir host and transmits it to others. Incorrect Options The remaining options fail to match the well-established roles in the JE cycle: • B. A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 incorrectly identifies the Pig (A?3) as the reservoir and Birds (B?4) as the amplifier. Pigs are the amplifier, and Birds are the reservoir. • C. A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4 incorrectly identifies the Human (A?2) as the reservoir and Birds (D?4) as the vector. Humans are accidental hosts, and the Culex mosquito is the vector. • D. A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2 incorrectly swaps the accidental host and the vector: it matches Humans (C?1) with the Culex mosquito and the Accidental host (D?2) with the Human.

questions.stemHtml: Female presented to OPD with vaginal discharge and itching. Smear finding shown in the image revealed the diagnosis. Choose the correct pathogen.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) The image displays a Papanicolaou (Pap) smear or a similar vaginal wet mount showing squamous epithelial cells that are diffusely covered with small, Gram-variable or basophilic (blue/purple) bacilli. These cells, obscured by the bacteria, are known as clue cells. • Clue Cells: The presence of clue cells (vaginal epithelial cells stippled with adhering bacteria) is the classic and definitive microscopic finding for Bacterial Vaginosis (BV), which is caused by a polymicrobial shift, but is primarily associated with the overgrowth of *Gardnerella vaginalis* (a small, facultatively anaerobic bacterium). Incorrect Options • A. Trichomonas: This protozoan causes trichomoniasis. The smear would show characteristic pear-shaped organisms with flagella (though flagella may be hard to see) and often numerous PMNs, but clue cells are not the primary diagnostic feature. • B. Candida: This fungus causes vulvovaginal candidiasis. The smear would typically show pseudohyphae (long filamentous forms) and budding yeast cells, which are absent in the image. • D. Doderlein bacillus: This refers to the large, Gram-positive Lactobacillus species, which are the dominant and protective flora in a healthy vagina. An abundance of Doderlein bacilli is an indicator of health, whereas the image shows a shift away from this dominant flora (Bacterial Vaginosis).

questions.stem: RNA virus diagnosis
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Reverse Transcription-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) is the gold standard for detecting and quantifying the genetic material of RNA viruses (e.g., SARS-CoV-2, Influenza, HIV). 1. Reverse Transcription (RT): Since PCR requires a DNA template, the first step involves using the enzyme Reverse Transcriptase to synthesize a complementary DNA (cDNA) strand from the viral RNA genome. 2. Amplification (PCR): Once cDNA is made, standard PCR is performed to exponentially amplify the target gene sequence, making it detectable and quantifiable. Other Options • A. Real Time PCR: This refers to the method of performing PCR (amplification and detection occur simultaneously). When applied to an RNA virus, it's called Real-Time RT-PCR (or qRT-PCR), so this is an incomplete description of the overall process. • C. Identification and amplification: This is a very general description. RT-PCR is the specific technique used for the identification and amplification of an RNA virus.

questions.stem: HBV subunit vaccine contains
questions.solutionHtml: n: • The hepatitis B subunit vaccine is a recombinant vaccine. • It contains hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), which stimulates the body to produce protective antibodies (anti-HBs). • This provides immunity against HBV without exposure to the live virus. Incorrect Options: • HBeAg ? Marker of viral replication; not used in vaccine. • HBcAg ? Core antigen; internal to virion; not included. • HBxAg ? Regulatory protein; not part of vaccine.

questions.stem: A 14 days old neonate developed conjunctivitis followed by pneumonitis showing bilateral infiltrated and TLC showing lymphocytic predominance. What may the etiological agent?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) • Chlamydia trachomatis is a common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia in infants born to infected mothers. • Neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis usually develops 1–2 weeks after birth, and pneumonia may follow, typically at 2–12 weeks of age. • Clinical clues: o Conjunctivitis without significant purulence o Pneumonitis with bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest X-ray o Lymphocytic predominance in the blood count (unlike bacterial infections with neutrophilia) • Treatment: oral erythromycin or azithromycin. Incorrect Options: A. Mycoplasma pneumoniae • Causes atypical pneumonia in older children and adults, rarely in neonates. • Neonatal age and presence of conjunctivitis are not typical. B. Haemophilus influenzae • Causes bacterial pneumonia, often severe with neutrophilic response. • Rarely causes neonatal conjunctivitis. C. Streptococcus pneumoniae • Usually causes acute bacterial pneumonia with fever, tachypnea, and neutrophilia. • Not associated with neonatal conjunctivitis or lymphocytic predominance.

questions.stem: Only AntiHBc-IgG +ve, what is the stage of the disease
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) • Anti-HBc IgG is a marker of previous or resolved HBV infection. • If anti-HBc IgG is the only positive marker (i.e., HBsAg and anti-HBs are negative), it usually indicates remote or past infection. • This pattern is sometimes called “isolated anti-HBc IgG”, and in most cases, it reflects resolved infection with waning anti-HBs. • No active viral replication is present, so no ongoing hepatitis is implied. Incorrect Options: A. Chronic hepatitis active phase ? • Would show HBsAg positive, sometimes HBeAg positive, and often elevated liver enzymes. C. Chronic hepatitis with pre-mutant core ? • Rare scenario with HBsAg positive, anti-HBc positive, and specific mutations in the precore region; anti-HBc IgG alone is insufficient to diagnose this. D. Acute hepatitis ? • Usually has anti-HBc IgM positive, often HBsAg positive, and elevated liver enzymes.

questions.stemHtml: HIV positive patient with diarrhoea. Stool examination, acid fast stain shows 8 -10 micrometer oocyst as shown in the image. Choose the correct pathogen.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) The clinical presentation of an HIV-positive patient with diarrhea points toward an opportunistic intestinal infection, and the microscopic findings confirm the diagnosis. The image shows several spherical, acid-fast oocysts that are approximately 8-10 micrometers (?m) in diameter. This size and appearance is characteristic of Cyclospora cayetanensis. The oocysts of Cyclospora are modified acid-fast positive (appearing bright red/pink against a blue background, as shown) and are significantly larger than those of Cryptosporidium but smaller than those of Cystoisospora. The typical size range for Cyclospora is 8?10 ?m, precisely matching the description in the prompt. Incorrect Options • B. Cryptosporidium: This protozoan is a common cause of severe, chronic diarrhea in HIV patients. However, its oocysts are much smaller, typically 4?6 ?m in diameter, and stain fully acid-fast. • C. Cystoisospora (Isospora): This protozoan causes cystoisosporiasis. Its oocysts are distinctly larger and oval (ellipsoidal), measuring around 20?30 ?m in length, which is much larger than the 8?10 ?m size described. • D. Microsporidium: These are spore-forming fungi. Their spores are tiny, ranging from 1?4 ?m, and are therefore much smaller than the organism described. They are often visualized using specific stains like modified trichrome, rather than the acid-fast stain shown here.

questions.stemHtml: H/o trauma six weeks ago. Lymphatic spread of the lesion has shown in the image. All the organisms have the property of lymphatic spread except
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Corynebacterium minutissimum. Nocardia brasiliensis: This bacterium can cause nocardiosis. Classic erythema infectiosum in children o Red cell aplasia ? In immunocompromised patients, transient aplastic crises can occur o Nonimmune fetal hydrops ? questions.stemHtml: HPE of warty verrucous lesions of the foot shown in the image. Choose the true statement.

options.label: C
options.text: Sclerotic bodies formed due to macrophages

options.label: D
options.text: It is caused by a Yeast

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) The image shows a histology section of a warty lesion containing a cluster of thick-walled, spherical, brown cells known as sclerotic bodies or Medlar bodies. The presence of sclerotic bodies is pathognomonic for Chromoblastomycosis. The fungi that cause Chromoblastomycosis (e.g., Fonsecaea pedrosoi, Cladophialophora carrionii) are characterized by having naturally pigmented cell walls due to the production of melanin. Fungi that produce dark pigment are classified as dematiaceous fungi (from the Greek dematios meaning black or brown). The brown color of the sclerotic bodies in the tissue section is a direct result of this intrinsic pigmentation. Incorrect Statements • A. Causes invasive lesions in immunocompromised: FALSE. Chromoblastomycosis is a chronic localized subcutaneous mycosis that is rarely invasive or disseminated, even in immunocompromised patients. The major dematiaceous fungus that causes invasive, systemic lesions in the immunocompromised is Exserohilum or similar species, not the primary agents of chromoblastomycosis. • C. Sclerotic bodies formed due to macrophages: FALSE. Sclerotic bodies are the fungal cells themselves, representing the specific morphological form the fungus takes within the host tissue. They are found within giant cells or microabscesses, but they are fungal structures, not host cells (macrophages) that have undergone a transformation. • D. It is caused by a Yeast: FALSE. While the sclerotic bodies are roughly spherical (yeast-like), the causative organisms of chromoblastomycosis are true molds in culture (forming septate hyphae). The sclerotic body is a unique, non-budding, tissue-specific morphology that divides by septation, which distinguishes it from typical budding yeast forms.

questions.stem: Choose the agent which acts both as disinfectant and antiseptic
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) • Ethanol is a broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent. • It can be used as an antiseptic on skin and mucous membranes (e.g., hand rubs, pre-injection skin prep). • It also acts as a disinfectant for inanimate surfaces and instruments at appropriate concentrations (60–90%). • Its mechanism involves protein denaturation and membrane disruption. Incorrect Options: B. Glutaraldehyde ? Strong disinfectant and sterilant, but too toxic to use on living tissue, so not an antiseptic. C. Orthophthaldehyde ? Used as a high-level disinfectant for instruments, but not applied to skin. D. Autoclave ? Physical method of sterilization using steam under pressure; not a chemical antiseptic.

questions.stem: Inclusion body in neutrophils seen in which rickettsial disease.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) • Anaplasma phagocytophilum causes Human Granulocytic Anaplasmosis (HGA). • The bacteria infect neutrophils and form morulae, which are inclusion bodies visible on Giemsa-stained blood smears. • Clinical features include fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and mild transaminitis. • This is a granulocytic infection, distinguishing it from other rickettsial infections that target endothelial cells or monocytes. Incorrect Options: A. Rickettsia rickettsii ? Causes Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, infects endothelial cells, not neutrophils. B. Rickettsia akari ? Causes rickettsialpox, infects endothelial cells, no neutrophil inclusions. D. Ehrlichia ? Causes Human Monocytic Ehrlichiosis (HME), infects monocytes, forming morulae in monocytes, not neutrophils.

questions.stemHtml: Inclusion bodies seen in Molluscum contagiosum is
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) The image shows the clinical presentation of Molluscum contagiosum, which is characterized by multiple, small, flesh-colored to pearly, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication. The causative agent is the Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a member of the Poxviridae family. Histological examination of these lesions reveals large, eosinophilic to basophilic, intracytoplasmic viral inclusion bodies within the epidermal cells. These are specifically named Henderson-Patterson bodies (or Molluscum bodies) and represent areas of massive viral replication within the keratinocytes. Their presence is diagnostic for Molluscum contagiosum. Incorrect Options • B. Multinucleated giant cell: These are characteristic of Herpes simplex virus (HSV) or Varicella-Zoster virus (VZV) infections (seen on a Tzanck smear) but are not the specific inclusion bodies for MCV. • C. Torres bodies: These are large, intracytoplasmic inclusions found in the liver cells of humans and animals infected with the Yellow Fever virus. • D. Ashcoff bodies: These are collections of inflammatory cells (t-lymphocytes, plasma cells, and Anitschkow cells) found in the connective tissue of the heart, which are pathognomonic for Rheumatic Fever. They are not viral inclusion bodies.

questions.stemHtml: Match the following
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) This option accurately pairs each specialized cell type with its primary anatomical location: • A. Clara cells match 2. Bronchiole (A?2). Clara cells (now often called Club cells) are non-ciliated, dome-shaped cells found in the epithelial lining of the terminal bronchioles. They secrete a component of surfactant and detoxify inhaled xenobiotics via Cytochrome P450 enzymes. • B. Parietal cells match 3. Stomach fundus (B?3). Parietal cells (Oxyntic cells) are found primarily in the gastric glands of the stomach body and fundus. They are responsible for secreting hydrochloric acid (HCl) and intrinsic factor. • C. Dust cells match 4. Lung (C?4). Dust cells is a common name for the Alveolar Macrophages found within the alveoli of the lungs. Their function is to phagocytose inhaled particles (like dust or soot) and microorganisms. • D. Kupffer cells match 1. Liver (D?1). Kupffer cells are specialized macrophages that reside in the liver's sinusoids. They function as part of the reticuloendothelial system, clearing blood of foreign material and old red blood cells. Incorrect Options The other options contain multiple incorrect pairings, failing to match the specific locations of these key cells: • B. A3 B2 C4 D1 incorrectly assigns Clara cells (A?3) to the stomach fundus (location of Parietal cells) and Parietal cells (B?2) to the bronchiole (location of Clara cells). • C. A2 B3 C1 D4 incorrectly assigns Dust cells (C?1) to the liver (location of Kupffer cells) and Kupffer cells (D?4) to the lung (location of Dust cells/Alveolar macrophages). • D. A2 B4 C3 D1 incorrectly assigns Parietal cells (B?4) to the lung and Dust cells (C?3) to the stomach fundus.

questions.stem: All the following are released from Th1 except
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Th1 cells are involved in cell-mediated immunity, important against intracellular pathogens (e.g., viruses, certain bacteria). • Th1 cytokines include: o IL-2: Stimulates T-cell proliferation o IFN-?: Activates macrophages, promotes IgG class switching • IL-12 is not secreted by Th1, but it is crucial for Th1 differentiation (produced by antigen-presenting cells). • IL-4 is a Th2 cytokine, promoting humoral immunity and class switching to IgE. Incorrect Options Explained: A. IL-2 ? Correctly secreted by Th1; stimulates T-cell proliferation and NK cell activation. B. IFN-? ? Major Th1 cytokine; activates macrophages and enhances cell-mediated immunity. D. IL-12 ? Produced by APCs; drives Th0 ? Th1 differentiation (not secreted by Th1 but essential for Th1 response).
