questions.solutionHtml: n: • HFMD is caused by Coxsackievirus A16 or Enterovirus 71. • Characteristic features: o Vesicular lesions on the hands, feet, and oral mucosa o Often accompanied by fever and malaise • The vesicles are painful or tender and may ulcerate in the mouth. • Diagnosis is usually clinical; self-limiting in most children. Incorrect Options: A. Roseola infantum ? • Caused by HHV-6/HHV-7 • Presents with high fever followed by a maculopapular rash, not vesicular. B. Dengue ? • Presents with petechial or maculopapular rash, not vesicular. C. Zika ? • Causes maculopapular rash, often pruritic, but not vesicular.

questions.stemHtml: A lesion on the back is shown in the image. Correct etiological agent is
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) The image displays a localized, ulcerated lesion with a central black, necrotic scab, known as an eschar. The presence of an eschar is a highly characteristic sign of infection by Orientia tsutsugamushi, the bacterium that causes Scrub typhus. This bacterium is transmitted via the bite of an infected larval mite (chigger). The eschar forms at the site of the chigger bite and often serves as a key diagnostic clue for this rickettsial disease, particularly in endemic areas of Asia and the Western Pacific. Incorrect Options • A. Covid 19: This is a viral respiratory disease caused by SARS-CoV-2. It does not typically present with a localized, necrotic eschar, though various non-specific skin rashes have been reported. • B. RMSF (Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever): RMSF is caused by Rickettsia rickettsii and transmitted by ticks. While it is a rickettsial disease, the characteristic skin finding is a maculopapular rash that typically begins on the ankles and wrists and spreads centrally. Eschar formation is rare in RMSF (unlike its African counterpart, African Tick-Bite Fever). • D. Malaria: This is a parasitic disease caused by Plasmodium species, transmitted by mosquitoes. The infection targets red blood cells and causes fever, chills, and organ damage. It does not cause localized eschar lesions.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the stain
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) The image displays a classic result of the Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain, also known as the acid-fast stain. This technique is used to identify bacteria, primarily mycobacteria (like Mycobacterium tuberculosis), that have high concentrations of mycolic acid in their cell walls, making them resistant to decolorization by acid-alcohol. 1. Appearance: The image shows slender, rod-shaped bacteria (bacilli) stained bright red/pink, while the background and non-acid-fast material are stained blue (the counterstain). 2. Principle: The red color is retained by the acid-fast organisms because the initial application of heat and concentrated primary stain (carbol fuchsin) allows the stain to penetrate the waxy cell wall, which then resists decolorization by the acid-alcohol wash. Incorrect Options • A. Albert stain: This stain is used to detect metachromatic granules (volutin granules) in Corynebacterium diphtheriae. The granules would stain blue/black, and the bacilli would stain green, which is not the pattern seen here. • C. Gram stain: This is the most common stain, differentiating bacteria into two groups. Gram-positive bacteria stain purple/blue, and Gram-negative bacteria stain red/pink. It does not typically reveal the combination of red bacilli on a blue background seen here, nor is it effective for mycobacteria. • D. Sudan black: This is a fat stain used to detect lipids (such as phospholipids or neutral fats) in cells, often used in hematology to differentiate leukemia types. It is not used for this type of bacterial identification.

questions.stem: Alcohol based sanitizer not useful in
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) • Alcohol-based sanitizers (60–90% ethanol or isopropanol) are effective against most bacteria and viruses on clean hands. • They are recommended: o Before patient contact (to prevent pathogen transmission) o After patient contact (to prevent cross-infection) • Limitation: They do not work effectively on hands that are visibly dirty or greasy because organic matter reduces their antimicrobial activity. • In such cases, handwashing with soap and water is required. Incorrect Options: A. Before examining a patient ? True, sanitizer is effective if hands are clean. B. After examining a patient ? True, sanitizer is effective on clean hands. D. None of the above ? Incorrect, because visibly soiled hands require soap and water.

questions.stem: Which of the following sterilization method can destroy spores
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Ethylene oxide (ETO) is a chemical sterilant used for heat- and moisture-sensitive medical equipment. • Mechanism: Alkylates proteins and DNA, effectively killing all microorganisms including bacterial spores. • It is widely used for surgical instruments, plastics, and electronics. Incorrect Options: B. Glutaraldehyde ? • High-level disinfectant, effective against bacteria, viruses, and some fungi. • Does not reliably kill bacterial spores without prolonged exposure (>10 hours). C. Pasteurization ? • Heat treatment (e.g., 63°C for 30 min) to reduce microbial load in liquids. • Does not kill spores, only vegetative bacteria. D. Tyndallization ? • Intermittent boiling over several days, kills vegetative bacteria, but may not reliably destroy all spores; less practical than ETO or autoclaving.

questions.stemHtml: Choose the egg for the parasite shown in the image
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) The egg labeled B is the correct egg for the genus Taenia (both T. solium and T. saginata have eggs that are morphologically identical). The key features are: 1. Shape: The egg is spherical or subspherical. 2. Shell: It has a thick, dark brown/yellow shell known as an embryophore. 3. Striations: The embryophore is characterized by conspicuous radial striations (lines radiating outward). 4. Contents: It contains a six-hooked embryo called an oncosphere or hexacanth embryo. This morphology, clearly seen in image B, is unique to Taenia eggs. Incorrect Options • A: This egg is large, thick-shelled, and typically brown with an operculum (lid), characteristic of Diphyllobothrium latum (Broad Fish Tapeworm) or an operculated trematode (fluke). • C: This egg is oval/ellipsoidal with a distinct operculum at one end, characteristic of an egg from a fluke (trematode), such as Clonorchis sinensis (Chinese Liver Fluke). • D: This egg is thin-shelled and contains an embryo that has already divided into blastomeres (usually 2 to 8 cells), which is the classic appearance of a Hookworm egg (Ancylostoma or Necator).

questions.stem: Choose the true statement:

options.label: A
options.text: Fasciola buski resides in intrahepatic radicles

options.label: C
options.text: F. hepatica infection through infected water caltrops

questions.answerText: F. hepatica infection through infected water caltrops
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Fasciola hepatica (common liver fluke) infects humans via ingestion of water plants (e.g., watercress, water caltrops) contaminated with metacercariae. • It resides in the intrahepatic bile ducts, not the gut lumen. • Treatment: Triclabendazole is effective for Fasciola spp., but not for all trematodes. ? Incorrect Options: A. F. buski resides in intrahepatic radicles ? FALSE • Fasciola buski inhabits the small intestine, not the liver. B. Triclabendazole doc for all trematodes ? FALSE • Triclabendazole is specifically for Fasciola spp. and some Paragonimus spp. • Other trematodes (e.g., Schistosoma) require praziquantel. D. S. haematobium is monoecious ? FALSE • Schistosoma haematobium is dioecious (separate male and female worms), unlike most other trematodes.

questions.stem: Mucormycosis- which layer of fungal cell wall / membrane is absent:
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Mucorales (agents of mucormycosis) have chitin and chitosan in their cell walls and ergosterol in the membrane, but they lack significant amounts of 1,3-?-D-glucan. • This is clinically important because antifungal drugs like echinocandins, which inhibit ?-D-glucan synthesis, are ineffective against mucormycosis. • Treatment usually relies on amphotericin B or posaconazole. Incorrect Options: A. Chitin ? Present in Mucorales cell wall; provides structural support. C. Mannan ? Found in fungal cell walls, especially in yeasts; may be present in small amounts. D. Ergosterol ? Present in fungal cell membrane; target of amphotericin B and azoles.

questions.stem: A boy came with intractable diarrhea after a beach trip. Stool is watery and smell of rice. Pathogen affect which cell adhesion molecule:
questions.solutionHtml: n: • The classic rice-water diarrhea after a beach trip suggests Vibrio cholerae infection. • V. cholerae produces cholera toxin, which: o Increases cAMP in enterocytes o Activates CFTR chloride channels, leading to massive Cl? and water secretion • This results in disruption of tight junctions between enterocytes, increasing paracellular permeability and contributing to profuse watery diarrhea. • Tight junctions normally seal the space between epithelial cells, maintaining selective barrier function, so their disruption leads to fluid loss into the intestinal lumen. Incorrect Options: A. Gap junction ? • Gap junctions allow direct communication between adjacent cells via ion and small molecule transfer. • Not the primary target in cholera or similar secretory diarrheas. C. Hemidesmosome ? • Anchors epithelial cells to the basement membrane. • Involved in structural adhesion, not water secretion or diarrhea. D. Zona adherens (adherens junction) ? • Connects actin cytoskeletons of adjacent cells; important for cell-cell adhesion but not the main target in cholera-induced diarrhea.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with submandibular region swelling. Lump formation after dental procedure. Yellow granules present in the discharge. Gram stain shown in the image. What is the pathogen responsible for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) The clinical presentation described is classic for Actinomycosis, specifically the cervicofacial form (Lumpy Jaw): 1. Clinical Features: The disease presents with a submandibular region swelling/lump, often with a preceding dental procedure (trauma allowing entry of the organism). 2. Diagnostic Sign: The discharge contains characteristic yellow granules (called sulfur granules). These are microcolonies of the bacteria embedded in host material and are pathognomonic for actinomycosis. 3. Microscopy: The image shows Gram-positive (staining purple/blue), non-spore-forming bacteria that are highly filamentous, branching rods. This "mold-like" or fungal appearance is characteristic of the filamentous bacterium Actinomyces israelii. Actinomyces israelii is an anaerobic or microaerophilic commensal of the oral cavity. Trauma, like a tooth extraction, allows it to invade deeper tissues, leading to a chronic, suppurative infection. Incorrect Options • A. Bacillus anthracis: This bacterium is Gram-positive and rod-shaped, but it forms spores and does not typically exhibit the extensive branching filamentous morphology seen in the image. It causes anthrax (cutaneous, inhalation, or gastrointestinal). • C. Candida albicans: This is a fungus. In a Gram stain, it would appear as large, Gram-positive budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae. It is not a filamentous, branching rod like Actinomyces. • D. Staphylococcus aureus: This bacterium is Gram-positive and appears as spherical cells (cocci) arranged in characteristic grape-like clusters, not the branching rods shown in the image. It causes acute, pyogenic (pus-forming) abscesses, but rarely the chronic, indurated swelling with sulfur granules typical of actinomycosis.

questions.stemHtml: A child admitted with the features of meningitis and CSF Gram stain shown in the image. Choose correct Property of the bacteria
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcus) is the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in children (and adults) and possesses two definitive properties used for its laboratory identification: 1. Optochin Sensitive: S. pneumoniae is sensitive to the chemical Optochin (ethylhydrocupreine hydrochloride). When a paper disk containing Optochin is placed on a culture plate, the growth of S. pneumoniae is inhibited, forming a zone of clearance. This is the primary test to distinguish it from other ?-hemolytic streptococci. 2. Catalase Negative: Like all species in the genus Streptococcus, S. pneumoniae lacks the enzyme catalase, meaning it does not produce bubbles when hydrogen peroxide is added to a colony. This test differentiates Streptococci (catalase negative) from Staphylococci (catalase positive). Incorrect Options • B. Oxidase positive: This is a key property of Gram-negative diplococci like Neisseria meningitidis (another common cause of meningitis) and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. S. pneumoniae is Oxidase negative. • C. Ferments glucose: While S. pneumoniae is capable of fermenting glucose, this property is common to many bacteria and is not specific or diagnostic enough to distinguish it from other Gram-positive cocci. • D. Mannose sensitive: This is not a standard or clinically relevant biochemical property used for the definitive identification or differentiation of S. pneumoniae in a diagnostic setting.

questions.stem: Smoker with pneumonia diagnosed as mycotic endocarditis. what may be the GMS stain finding?

options.label: B
options.text: Non septate hyphae with vertical branching

questions.solutionHtml: n: • The description points toward Aspergillus species, which can cause fungal endocarditis and pulmonary infection. • Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) stain highlights fungal cell walls, showing: o Septate hyphae o Acute-angle (dichotomous) branching (~45°) • Aspergillus infections are more common in immunocompromised patients, smokers with underlying lung disease, or those with prosthetic valves. Incorrect Options: B. Non-septate hyphae with vertical branching ? • Characteristic of Mucorales (Mucor, Rhizopus). • Branching is irregular, right-angled (90°), not dichotomous. C. Yeast with capsule ? • Describes Cryptococcus neoformans; GMS highlights budding yeasts with thick capsule. • Does not produce septate hyphae. D. Figure-of-eight appearance ? • Seen in Scedosporium species or sometimes in Blastomyces in tissue; not typical for Aspergillus.

questions.stemHtml: The below is the life cycle of which organism
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) • Nipah virus is a zoonotic virus from the Paramyxoviridae family. • Natural reservoir: Fruit bats (Pteropus species). • Transmission: o From bats to humans indirectly via pigs (amplifying host) or contaminated fruits/vegetables. o Direct human-to-human transmission can occur in healthcare settings. • The life cycle shown in the image depicts: bats ? fruits/pigs ? humans, which is classic for Nipah virus outbreaks in Malaysia, Bangladesh, and India. • Clinical features: Encephalitis, respiratory symptoms, high mortality. Incorrect Options: B. Ebola virus ? • Filovirus causing hemorrhagic fever. • Transmission mainly through direct contact with blood or body fluids of infected humans or animals (e.g., primates, not bats via fruit). C. Japanese Encephalitis Virus ? • Flavivirus transmitted by Culex mosquitoes from pigs or birds to humans. • Humans are dead-end hosts; not transmitted via bats or fruit. D. Zika virus ? • Flavivirus transmitted primarily by Aedes mosquitoes. • Not zoonotic through pigs or bats; mainly associated with mosquito bites.

questions.stem: A known case of HIV/AIDS patient with diarrhea. On Kinyoun stain there were plenty of oocysts ranging in size from 4 to 6 microns. Your most probable diagnosis is?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Cryptosporidium is a common opportunistic protozoal infection in HIV/AIDS patients, particularly when the CD4 count is low. It causes chronic, watery diarrhea and can lead to significant dehydration. On Kinyoun stain (an acid-fast stain), Cryptosporidium oocysts appear as small, round to slightly oval structures, typically 4–6 microns in size, which matches the description in this patient. This size range is characteristic and helps distinguish it from other coccidian parasites. Incorrect Options: A. Balantidium – Balantidium coli is a large ciliate protozoan, usually much bigger than 50 microns, causing dysentery-like symptoms. Its size and morphology do not match the 4–6 micron oocysts seen on Kinyoun stain. C. Cyclospora – Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts are larger, about 8–10 microns, and also stain variably with acid-fast stains. The smaller size (4–6 microns) in this case rules out Cyclospora. D. Cystoisospora (formerly Isospora) – Cystoisospora belli oocysts are bigger, typically 20–30 microns, and elliptical. Again, the small size described excludes this organism.

questions.stemHtml: A young male presented with skin lesions as shown below. Which of the following is not responsible for the condition
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) The correct answer is D. Aspergillus. Aspergillus species are common environmental molds that primarily cause invasive infections (e.g., aspergillosis, including invasive pulmonary aspergillosis) in immunocompromised patients. They may also cause allergic syndromes but are not dermatophytes and do not cause the superficial skin infections known as Tinea or ringworm. Therefore, Aspergillus is not responsible for the lesion pictured. Incorrect Options The lesions shown, characterized by annular (ring-shaped) erythematous plaques with raised, vesicular borders and central clearing , are caused by dermatophytes (fungi that thrive on keratinized tissue). Options A, B, and C are all genera of dermatophytes and are responsible for Tinea infections: • A. Trichophyton: This genus is the most common cause of Tinea infections globally, including Tinea corporis, Tinea pedis, and Tinea capitis. • B. Epidermophyton: This genus contains one pathogenic species, Epidermophyton floccosum, which causes Tinea pedis, Tinea cruris, and Tinea corporis. • C. Microsporum: This genus is primarily known for causing Tinea capitis (scalp ringworm) but also causes Tinea corporis.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with complaint of dysphagia. On UGI endoscopy a diagnosis of oesophageal candidiasis was made. The organism obtained from the sample was cultured on a specialized medium and the findings shown below were visible on microscopy of the culture. What phenomenon is shown below?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) The image displays a characteristic germ tube—a slender, tube-like outgrowth that lacks a constriction at its base where it emerges from the parent yeast cell. This test is a rapid, preliminary identification method for Candida albicans, the species most frequently responsible for candidiasis (including esophageal candidiasis, particularly in immunocompromised patients). The test involves incubating a sample of the yeast in serum for about 2 to 3 hours at 37?C. The formation of a germ tube under these conditions is a strong presumptive identification for C. albicans because most other Candida species do not form them. Incorrect Options • B. Spore formation: True spores (such as blastospores, arthrospores, or chlamydospores) represent dormant or reproductive structures. The structure shown is an initial hyphal element (germ tube) for tissue invasion, not a spore. • C. Mould to yeast formation: This refers to the process of dimorphism, where a fungus changes its form in response to environmental temperature (e.g., Histoplasma grows as a mold at 25?C and yeast at 37?C). While C. albicans exhibits dimorphism (growing as yeast and hyphae/pseudohyphae), the image specifically shows the initiation of the hyphal form from the yeast cell, which is the germ tube test. • D. Budding: Budding is the typical asexual reproduction method for yeast, resulting in daughter cells that detach or remain attached as pseudohyphae. While the yeast cell at the base of the germ tube would have divided by budding, the phenomenon highlighted by the outgrowth is germ tube formation.

questions.stemHtml: A young male presented with fever, hepato-splenomegaly. On investigation the person showed the below organism. Which of the following is true regarding the same?

options.label: A
options.text: Rk139 can be detected in blood and bone marrow sample

options.label: B
options.text: Being obligate intracellular it can only be cultured in cell free medium

options.label: D
options.text: The organism can be better demonstrated in buffy coat preparations

questions.answerText: The organism can be better demonstrated in buffy coat preparations
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) The statement is TRUE. Leishmania amastigotes, also known as Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies, are found primarily within the macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system (e.g., bone marrow, spleen, and liver). When preparing a peripheral blood smear, the total number of infected monocytes/macrophages is low. However, concentrating the blood through centrifugation allows the isolation of the buffy coat (the layer of white blood cells), which contains the highest concentration of LD body-laden macrophages, significantly improving the yield for microscopic diagnosis compared to a standard peripheral blood smear. Incorrect Options • A. Rk139 can be detected in blood and bone marrow sample: FALSE. The correct antigen is rk39. Furthermore, the rk39 test is an antibody (serological) test done on blood (serum), not a direct detection of the antigen in bone marrow. • B. Being obligate intracellular it can only be cultured in cell free medium: FALSE. Leishmania is an obligate intracellular parasite in its amastigote form within the human host. However, it can be cultured in vitro by converting its form into the motile promastigote stage in cell-free media (like NNN medium), not a cell culture medium as the statement implies. • C. Amastigotes show diurnal periodicity: FALSE. Diurnal periodicity (the cyclical appearance of organisms in the blood at specific times of the day) is a key feature of the microfilariae of some filarial worms (like Wuchereria bancrofti), not the amastigote stage of Leishmania. Amastigotes are stationary within tissue cells.

questions.stemHtml: The cell wall shown below belongs to which organism?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Neisseria meningitidis Neisseria meningitidis, often referred to as meningococcus, is a Gram negative bacterium that can cause meningitis and other forms of meningococcal disease such as meningococcemia, a life-threatening sepsis. Lipooligosaccharide is present in the outer membrane of Neisseria. It acts like an endotoxin and is responsible for septic shock. Other virulence features are polysaccharide capsule, that prevents its phagocytosis and aids evasion by host immune system. Adhesion is another key virulence feature to successfully invade host cell. There are many such proteins, including Pili which mediate attachment of the bacteria to the epithelial lining of the nasopharynx.

questions.stem: Gram positive bacilli isolated from a child, that is motile at 22 degrees and non-motile at 37 degrees is-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Listeria monocytogenes Listeria monocytogenes is a Gram positive bacterium, and a facultative anaerobic bacterium, capable of surviving in the presence or absence of oxygen. It exhibits differential motility, that is, it grows at 22 degrees and not at 37 degrees. It exhibits a tumbling type of motility. Its ability to grow at temperatures as low as 0 °C permits multiplication at typical refrigeration temperatures, greatly increasing its ability to evade control in human foodstuffs. It can cause meningitis in neonates, cancer and transplant patients. It can also produce Granulomatum infantiseptica.

questions.stemHtml: Which haematological manifestation associated with this image ?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Pure red cell aplasia The given image shows “Slapped cheek appearance” seen in Erythema infectiosum. This is caused by Parvovirus B19, which is a non-enveloped ss DNA virus. Other associations of Parvovirus are Non-immune fetal hydrops, polyarthritis in adults, blueberry muffin rash and Pure red cell aplasia causing aplastic crisis.

questions.stem: Infective form of toxoplasmosis to humans from cat feces is-
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer (A)

Oocyst

Toxoplasma gondii is a protozoan parasite that infects most species of warm-blooded animals, including humans, and causes the disease toxoplasmosis.

The only known definitive hosts for Toxoplasma gondii are members of family Felidae (domestic cats and their relatives). Humans can become infected by any of several routes:

•    Eating undercooked meat of animals harboring tissue cysts   .

•    Consuming food or water contaminated with cat feces or by contaminated environmental samples (such as fecal-contaminated soil or changing the litter box of a pet cat)   .

•    Blood transfusion or organ transplantation   .

•    Transplacentally from mother to fetus   .

questions.stem: Protozoan pathogen found in Kupffer cells is-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Leishmania Leishmaniasis is caused by protozoa of genus Leishmania. It is transmitted by the bite of female Phlebotomus sandfly. The lifecycle of Leishmania includes two forms: Promastigote (in sandfly vector) and Amastigote (in the reticuloendothelial cells of the host). The amastigote form is also known as Leishmania-Donovan (LD) body. It is an intracellular form inside the macrophages. Kupffer cells are the macrophages of the liver. Plasmodium and Babesia are present in RBCs. Giardia is a free protozoa, not intracellular.

questions.stemHtml: Choose the correct incubation periods
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) This option correctly pairs each disease with its typical incubation period, the time from exposure to the first appearance of symptoms. • A. Hepatitis A matches 2. 15-45 days (A?2). The average incubation period for Hepatitis A is approximately 28 days, but it can range from 15 to 50 days. • B. Varicella matches 3. 14-21 days (B?3). The incubation period for chickenpox, caused by the Varicella-zoster virus, is typically 14 to 16 days, with a range of 10 to 21 days. • C. COVID 19 matches 4. 1-10 days (C?4). The median incubation period for COVID-19 is estimated to be around 4-5 days, with a range of 1 to 14 days, though some sources state a maximum of 10 days. • D. Syphilis matches 1. 9-90 days (D?1). The primary stage of syphilis develops after an average incubation period of 21 days, with a very wide range of 10 to 90 days. Incorrect Options Other options B. A-2, B-4, C-1, D-2 incorrectly pairs Varicella with 10 days (B?4) and Hepatitis A with 15-45 days (A?2). The 10-day period is too short for Varicella. • C. A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4 incorrectly pairs COVID-19 with 9-90 days (C?1) and Syphilis with 1-10 days (D?4). COVID-19's incubation is much shorter and Syphilis' is much longer. • D. A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4 incorrectly pairs Hepatitis A with 9-90 days (A?1). This period is far too long for Hepatitis A.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the pathogen:
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Aspergillus The hyphae of the fungus in the given diagram are septate and have acute angle branching. That is suggestive of Aspergillus. Mucor have aseptate hyphae with obtuse angle branching. Aspergillus can cause a variety of infections in the human body such as- • Acute invasive aspergillosis, a form that grows into surrounding tissue, more common in those with weakened immune systems such as AIDS or chemotherapy patients • Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, which affects patients with respiratory diseases such as asthma, cystic fibrosis, and sinusitis • Aspergilloma, a "fungus ball" that can form within cavities such as the lung • Disseminated invasive aspergillosis, an infection spread widely through the body

questions.stemHtml: A woman from Tamil Nadu presents with a mass protruding from her nose. What is the pathogen implicated in this case?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Rhinosporidium seeberi Rhinosporidiosis is an infection caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi. Rhinosporidiosis is a granulomatous disease affecting the mucous membrane of nasopharynx, oropharynx, conjunctiva, rectum and external genitalia. Though the floor of the nose and inferior turbinate are the most common sites, the lesions may appear elsewhere too. Traumatic inoculation from one site to others is common. On histopathology, thick walled sporangia with 1000+ endospores, each 6 - 10 microns, accompanied by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate is seen. Treatment is by surgical excision.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient with immunocompromised state presents with a fungal infection. On biopsy, budding cells with pseudohyphae were present. What is the condition indicated?
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer (A)

Invasive candidiasis

Invasive candidiasis is an infection that can be caused by various species of Candida yeast. Many species of Candida are harmless commensals or endosymbionts of hosts including humans; however, when mucosal barriers are disrupted or the immune system is compromised they can invade and cause disease, known as an opportunistic infection.

The diagram given below shows the budding yeast cells of Candida.

questions.stem: Serial dilutions of agglutination test is given here. Negative till 1:40 dilution is due to:
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Excess antibody The reason for positive sample on serial dilutions is called Prozone phenomenon and it occurs to due to excess antibodies as compared with the antigens. On further dilution, there is equal number of Ab and Ag, which produce a lattice and is visible as positive. However on diluting further, Antigens will outnumber the antigens, called Postzone phenomenon. Pro and Postzone phenomenon are false negative.

questions.stem: A patient presents with bloody dysentery. Imaging reveals a liver abscess in the right lobe of the liver with irregular margins. What is the condition?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Amoebic liver abscess A amoebic liver abscess is a type of liver abscess caused by amebiasis. It is the involvement of liver tissue by trophozoites of the organism Entamoeba histolytica. Approximately 90% of patients with E histolytica are asymptomatic. The two most common manifestations of E histolytica include colitis (bloody stool with mucus, abdominal pain, and/or diarrhea), and discovery of a liver abscess on imaging. Liver abscess commonly present as right upper quadrant abdominal pain and fever, with worsening features associated with abscess rupture.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not transmitted perinatally?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Rubella Rubella is an acute, contagious viral infection. While rubella virus infection usually causes a mild fever and rash in children and adults, infection during pregnancy, especially during the first trimester, can result in miscarriage, fetal death, stillbirth, or infants with congenital malformations, known as congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). If infection occurs 0–11 weeks after conception, the infant has a 90% risk of being affected. If the infection occurs 12–20 weeks after conception, the risk is 20%. Infants are not generally affected if rubella is contracted during the third trimester. The classic triad for congenital rubella syndrome is: • Sensorineural deafness • Eye abnormalities—especially retinopathy, cataract, glaucoma and microphthalmia. • Congenital heart disease—especially pulmonary artery stenosis and patent ductus arteriosus.

questions.stem: PCR which of the organism needed a step of reverse transcriptase
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) is a technique that amplifies DNA. However, many viruses, like Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), have a genome made of RNA rather than DNA. To detect these viruses using PCR, their RNA genome must first be converted into DNA. This conversion is performed by an enzyme called reverse transcriptase in a process known as reverse transcription. The resulting complementary DNA (cDNA) can then be amplified by standard PCR. This combined technique is known as reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR).

questions.stem: Cell to cell transfer of bacteria by actin filament is classically seen in
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answe-(C) Listeria monocytogenes is a facultative intracellular bacterium that has a unique mechanism to spread directly from one host cell to another. After entering a host cell, Listeria hijacks the host’s actin cytoskeleton to form “actin comet tails,” which propel the bacterium through the cytoplasm and into neighboring cells without exposure to the extracellular environment. This cell-to-cell transfer via actin filaments allows Listeria to evade the host immune system, which is why it’s a classic example of this mechanism. Incorrect Options: A. Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) – EIEC invades intestinal epithelial cells but does not use actin-based motility for cell-to-cell spread. Its mechanism is more similar to Shigella. B. Helicobacter pylori – H. pylori colonizes the gastric mucosa and produces virulence factors like urease, CagA, and VacA, but it does not utilize actin for intracellular motility or direct cell-to-cell transfer. D. Salmonella typhi – Salmonella invades intestinal epithelial cells and survives within phagosomes, but it does not form actin comet tails for spreading between cells. Its pathogenesis involves systemic dissemination rather than direct cell-to-cell spread.

questions.stemHtml: Which toxin acts by the MoA shown in the image.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) The image shows the mechanism of action of diphtheria toxin, which is produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It is an A-B exotoxin where the B subunit binds to the host cell membrane and facilitates entry of the A subunit. Once inside the cell, the A subunit catalyzes ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2 (EF-2) using NAD?. This modification inactivates EF-2, which is essential for protein synthesis at the ribosome. As a result, the cell is unable to synthesize proteins, leading to cell death. This classic mechanism is highly characteristic of diphtheria toxin and explains its cytotoxic effects. Incorrect Option: A. Vibrio cholerae Vibrio cholerae produces cholera toxin, which is also an A-B exotoxin but works through a different mechanism. It ADP-ribosylates the Gs alpha subunit, leading to persistent activation of adenylate cyclase. This increases intracellular cAMP levels, causing chloride and water secretion into the intestinal lumen and resulting in profuse watery diarrhea. It does not inhibit EF-2 or interfere with protein synthesis. Incorrect Option: B. Bacillus anthracis Bacillus anthracis produces anthrax toxin, which consists of three components: protective antigen, edema factor, and lethal factor. Edema factor acts as an adenylate cyclase, increasing cAMP levels, while lethal factor is a protease that inactivates MAP kinase signaling pathways. These effects lead to immune evasion, edema, and cell death but not via inhibition of EF-2 or protein synthesis machinery. Incorrect Option: D. Clostridium perfringens Clostridium perfringens primarily produces alpha toxin, which is a lecithinase (phospholipase C). This toxin causes cell membrane disruption by degrading phospholipids, leading to cell lysis and tissue necrosis, especially seen in gas gangrene. It does not target EF-2 or affect protein synthesis, so it is not the correct match for the image shown.

questions.stem: Which organism needs BSL 3
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) XDR TB. BSL-3 Organisms Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3) is required for work involving indigenous or exotic microbes that can cause serious or potentially lethal disease through aerosol transmission (inhalation). All work with these microbes must be performed in a biosafety cabinet. XDR TB (Extensively Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis) is caused by a strain of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an airborne pathogen that causes a serious, potentially lethal disease and is classified as a Risk Group 3 agent. This makes it a prime example of an organism requiring a BSL-3 laboratory.

questions.stemHtml: Image shown here is vector for all except
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answe-(A) The image shows a tick, which is a member of the Arachnid class. Ticks are known vectors for a wide range of diseases, including those caused by bacteria, protozoa, and viruses. However, Orientia tsutsugamushi, the bacterium that causes Scrub Typhus, is transmitted by the bite of an infected mite (specifically, the larval mite or chigger). A tick is a different arthropod vector and does not transmit this specific disease. Incorrect Options • B. Babesia microti: This is a protozoan parasite that causes babesiosis. It is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected deer tick (Ixodes scapularis). • C. Ehrlichia chaffeensis: This bacterium causes human monocytotropic ehrlichiosis. It is transmitted to humans by the bite of the Lone Star tick (Amblyomma americanum). • D. CCHF (Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever) virus: This is a bunyavirus that causes a severe hemorrhagic fever. It is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected tick, primarily those of the genus Hyalomma.

questions.stemHtml: A person living in a rural area comes to you with complaints of neck rigidity and fever. Hemiparesis present. Clinically diagnosed as encephalitis. H/o Swimming present. SEM image shown here. Choose the correct Pathogen.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Naegleria fowleri. The clinical presentation of a person with neck rigidity, fever, and hemiparesis is consistent with a diagnosis of encephalitis. The crucial clue is the history of swimming, which is the primary route of infection for Naegleria fowleri, the causative agent of a severe condition called Primary Amebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM). This amoeba is found in warm fresh water, and when it enters the nasal passages, it can travel to the brain. The provided SEM image is a classic depiction of the trophozoite stage of Naegleria fowleri, characterized by its distinctive eruptive pseudopods. The other options are less likely; Acanthamoeba and Balamuthia mandrillaris typically cause a slower, chronic form of encephalitis in immunocompromised individuals, and Giardia lamblia is a gastrointestinal parasite.

questions.stem: Which of the following structure is essential for permeating of viral RNA of HIV through membrane of host cell?
questions.solutionHtml: on: GP120 (Glycoprotein 120) is the surface glycoprotein of the HIV envelope. Its primary function is binding to the host cell's CD4 receptor and subsequently to a co-receptor (like CCR5 or CXCR4). While essential for the overall entry process by initiating attachment, GP120 itself does not directly mediate the fusion of the viral and host cell membranes or the permeation of the RNA. Option (C. CXCR5) Explanation: CXCR5 (C-X-C chemokine receptor type 5) is a host cell surface protein, not a viral structure. More importantly, while chemokine receptors are crucial co-receptors for HIV entry, CXCR5 is not one of the primary co-receptors (which are CCR5 and CXCR4) utilized by HIV for infection. Option (D. CCR4) Explanation: CCR4 (C-C chemokine receptor type 4) is also a host cell surface protein, not a viral structure. Similar to CXCR5, CCR4 is not a primary co-receptor used by HIV for entry. The main host co-receptors are CCR5 and CXCR4.

questions.stem: Vibrio cholera acts on disruption of which protein in tight junction?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answe-(D) Vibrio cholerae produces cholera toxin (CTX), which increases intracellular cAMP in intestinal epithelial cells. This leads to disruption of tight junctions and altered intestinal barrier function, causing massive watery diarrhea. The tight junctions are composed of proteins like occludin, claudins, and zonula occludens (ZO) proteins. Cholera toxin primarily affects occludin and ZO proteins, leading to increased paracellular permeability and secretory diarrhea. Incorrect Options: A. Cadherin – Cadherins are involved in adherens junctions, not tight junctions. They mediate cell–cell adhesion but are not the primary target of cholera toxin. B. Integrin – Integrins are cell–matrix adhesion molecules, not tight junction proteins. Vibrio cholerae does not act on integrins for diarrhea. C. Claudin – Claudins are structural components of tight junctions, but cholera toxin’s main effect is on occludins and ZO proteins, not claudins directly.

questions.stemHtml: A patient recently recovered from COVID19, Under Steroid treatment for 3 weeks came with headache and nasal discharge. Microscopy shown in the image. Identify the agent.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answe-(D) Correct Option: D. Mucor The clinical picture of a recently recovered COVID-19 patient who is under steroid treatment with symptoms of headache and nasal discharge is a classic presentation of Mucormycosis (Black Fungus). The image shows the characteristic histology of the causative fungi. 1. Clinical Correlation: COVID-19 patients, particularly those on steroids, are at high risk for Mucormycosis due to their immunocompromised state (steroids suppress the immune system) and the presence of high blood sugar. The fungus commonly infects the sinuses and spreads to the brain, causing headache and nasal discharge. 2. Histology: The image shows broad, ribbon-like, aseptate hyphae branching at right angles (90?), sometimes with irregular contours. This is the hallmark microscopic finding for the Mucorales order of fungi, which includes Mucor, Rhizopus, and Lichtheimia. Incorrect Options • A. Aspergillus: This is a common opportunistic fungus, but its hyphae are typically narrow, septate, and branch at acute angles (around 45?). This is a key distinguishing feature from Mucor. • B. Cryptococcus: This fungus is a budding yeast with a large capsule, causing meningitis and pulmonary infections. It does not form hyphae in tissue and has a completely different morphology. • C. Candida: This fungus typically appears in tissue as budding yeast and pseudohyphae, and sometimes true hyphae, but they are generally narrower than Mucor and have constrictions at the branching points.

questions.stem: HBsAg negative, Anti HBs Ag – Negative, Anti –HBc Total - positive, Anti HBc-IgM negative. Clinical stage
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answe-(B) The serological profile shows: • HBsAg negative ? No active hepatitis B infection. • Anti-HBs negative ? No protective antibodies from vaccination or recent recovery. • Anti-HBc total positive, Anti-HBc IgM negative ? Indicates past exposure to HBV. The total anti-HBc positivity reflects previous infection, while the absence of IgM indicates it is not an acute/recent infection. This pattern is classic for a resolved or past HBV infection, where the virus has been cleared but anti-HBc antibodies persist for life. Incorrect Options: A. Window period – During the window period, HBsAg is negative, anti-HBs is not yet detectable, and anti-HBc IgM is positive, reflecting acute infection. Here, IgM is negative, so this is not the window period. C. Chronic infection – Chronic hepatitis B is characterized by persistent HBsAg positivity for more than 6 months. HBsAg is negative here, so chronic infection is excluded. D. Vaccination – Vaccinated individuals show anti-HBs positivity without anti-HBc antibodies, since vaccination does not expose the person to the core antigen. Anti-HBc positivity here rules out vaccination

questions.stem: What are the advantages of saline wet mount over iodine wet mount? A. Motility can be studied better B. To stain nucleus and glycogen mass C. Bile-stained egg can be differentiated D. Cyst can be specifically identified by this method
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) A. Motility can be studied better Saline wet mount allows for the observation of motility in living organisms, such as protozoa (e.g., Giardia, Trichomonas). Because saline does not kill or alter the organisms, it allows them to remain alive, and their motility can be studied clearly. This is a distinct advantage over iodine wet mount, which tends to kill or immobilize the organisms due to its staining properties. C. Bile-stained egg can be differentiated Saline wet mount helps to differentiate bile-stained eggs in parasitic infections. The bile-stained eggs (e.g., from Ascaris lumbricoides or Clonorchis sinensis) are transparent, and in saline, they are easier to identify due to their natural appearance and the way the eggs react in a saline solution. Iodine may stain these eggs, making them harder to differentiate in certain cases, especially if the bile staining is subtle. Saline allows for a clearer, unstained view, which can be particularly helpful in bile-stained egg identification. Incorrect Answers: B. To stain nucleus and glycogen mass Iodine wet mount is specifically used for staining nuclei and glycogen masses, particularly in protozoa. The iodine solution stains these structures, making them more visible and easier to identify. Saline wet mount does not have this staining property and is used for observing live motile organisms or identifying cysts in their natural state, without staining. D. Cyst can be specifically identified by this method While saline wet mount can help in identifying the shape of cysts, iodine wet mount is typically preferred for highlighting and staining cyst walls and internal contents (e.g., glycogen masses and nuclei). The iodine stain makes these features stand out clearly, whereas saline allows the cyst to be seen but does not enhance the visualization of internal structures.

questions.stem: All the following tests are useful in 3-day duration of dengue fever except
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answe-(B) In the first 3 days of dengue fever, the infection is in its acute viremic phase, and the body has not yet produced significant IgM antibodies. Therefore, IgM capture ELISA is usually negative in this early period. Diagnostic tests that detect the virus directly, such as RT-PCR, NS1 antigen, or viral culture, are useful in the first few days of illness. Incorrect Options: A. RT-PCR – Detects viral RNA directly and is highly sensitive in the early viremic phase (first 5 days), making it useful in a 3-day illness. C. NS1 Antigen – NS1 is a nonstructural protein secreted by infected cells and can be detected from day 1 to 5 of illness, making it ideal for early diagnosis. D. Viral culture – Though less commonly used clinically due to complexity, viral culture can detect live virus during the early viremic phase, including day 3.

questions.stem: Neck stiffness, Kernig sign , Lymphocytosis, Glucose low, Protein High.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answe-(A) TB meningitis The CSF findings described—lymphocytic predominance, low glucose, and high protein—along with clinical features like neck stiffness and positive Kernig sign are classic for tuberculous meningitis (TBM). TBM usually has an insidious onset and is characterized by lymphocyte-predominant CSF, markedly raised protein, and low glucose due to consumption by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and inflammatory cells. Incorrect Options: B. Viral meningitis – Typically presents with lymphocytic predominance, but glucose is usually normal and protein is only mildly elevated. The severe glucose drop seen here is not characteristic. C. Fungal meningitis – Also shows lymphocytosis with low glucose and high protein, but fungal meningitis (e.g., Cryptococcus) is more common in immunocompromised patients and often has a more chronic course. TBM is more common in general populations. D. Pyogenic meningitis – Usually presents acutely with neutrophilic predominance, very low glucose, and high protein. The lymphocytic predominance in this case rules out pyogenic meningitis.

questions.stem: An Immunocompromised individual came with white patches in tongue which cannot be rubbed. Etiological agent is
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer (B)

In an immunocompromised individual, such as someone with HIV/AIDS, the appearance of white patches on the tongue that cannot be rubbed off is a classic sign of oral hairy leukoplakia. This condition is painless, typically appears along the sides (lateral borders) of the tongue, and is not removable by scraping. The cause of this condition is the Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), which becomes reactivated in immunosuppressed individuals. Unlike oral candidiasis (thrush), which is caused by Candida albicans and presents with removable white plaques, oral hairy leukoplakia is firmly attached to the mucosa due to thickening of the epithelium with viral involvement. It's important to distinguish this condition clinically because it often signals underlying immune deficiency, particularly HIV infection. Other options, such as HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus) or KSHV (Kaposi Sarcoma virus), present with painful ulcers or tumors, not white plaques that can't be scraped off. Therefore, EBV is the correct etiological agent.

questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer-(B)

These are features that suggest the patient may progress to severe dengue, and hospitalization is recommended.

Dengue Warning Signs include:

  1. Persistent vomiting
  2. Abdominal pain or tenderness

questions.stemHtml: Identify the toxin
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answe-(B) The diagram illustrates a toxin linking the T cell receptor (TCR) to the MHC class II molecule on an antigen-presenting cell (APC), outside of the normal antigen-binding groove. This mechanism is characteristic of a Superantigen. Streptococcus pyogenes produces several superantigens, including Streptococcal Pyrogenic Exotoxins ($\text{Spe}$s), which are responsible for toxic shock syndrome and scarlet fever rash. The action of superantigens is as follows: 1. They bind directly to the MHC II molecule (green structure on the APC) outside the peptide-binding cleft. 2. They simultaneously bind directly to the V? region of the TCR (blue structure on the T cell). 3. This cross-linking bypasses the need for specific antigen processing and presentation, leading to the massive, non-specific activation of up to 20% of the body's T cells. The resulting overwhelming release of cytokines (cytokine storm) causes the severe systemic symptoms seen in toxic shock syndrome. Incorrect Options • A. Cholera toxin: This is an AB toxin that acts on the intestinal lining. It enters the cell and permanently activates adenylate cyclase, leading to high levels of cyclic AMP (cAMP) and massive secretion of water and electrolytes. It has no superantigen activity. • C. Pseudomonas toxin: Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces Exotoxin A, which is an AB toxin that acts as an ADP-ribosyltransferase. It inactivates EF?2 (Elongation Factor 2), thereby inhibiting host protein synthesis. It has no superantigen activity. • D. E. coli labile toxin: LT (Labile Toxin) produced by ETEC is structurally and functionally similar to Cholera Toxin. It also permanently activates adenylate cyclase, causing elevated cAMP and watery diarrhea. It has no superantigen activity.

questions.stem: DOC for Enterococcus infective endocarditis, allergic to penicillin
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Vancomycin Enterococcus species are common causes of infective endocarditis. The drug of choice (DOC) for Enterococcal endocarditis is usually ampicillin or penicillin, often combined with gentamicin for synergistic bactericidal effect. However, in patients allergic to penicillin, vancomycin is the recommended alternative. Vancomycin is effective against penicillin-allergic patients and covers most Enterococcus strains causing endocarditis. Incorrect Options: B. Piperacillin – Although a broad-spectrum penicillin, it is contraindicated in patients with penicillin allergy. C. Aztreonam – A monobactam effective against Gram-negative bacteria but has no reliable activity against Enterococcus, so it is not suitable. D. Ceftriaxone – Cephalosporins generally have poor activity against Enterococcus and are not recommended as monotherapy, especially in endocarditis.

questions.stem: Which one of the following shows drug resistance?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) A. Donovanosis: Also known as granuloma inguinale, this sexually transmitted infection is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. It is typically responsive to antibiotics such as azithromycin, doxycycline, erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. While prolonged therapy is often required, significant drug resistance has not been widely reported. ? B. Syphilis: Caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, syphilis remains highly sensitive to penicillin. Penicillin G is the treatment of choice, and there have been no significant reports of resistance to this antibiotic. ? C. Gonorrhoea: Caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, this infection has developed resistance to multiple antibiotics over time, including penicillins, sulphonamides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and macrolides. The emergence of strains resistant to cephalosporins, particularly ceftriaxone, poses a significant public health challenge, as treatment options become increasingly limited. ? D. Chlamydia: Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, this infection is generally treated with antibiotics like azithromycin or doxycycline. While treatment failures can occur, widespread antibiotic resistance has not been a significant concern to date. ?

questions.stem: Which does not have polysaccharide capsule
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a DNA virus with an outer envelope containing surface antigens (HBsAg), but it does not have a polysaccharide capsule. Its structure is viral, not bacterial, so the concept of a polysaccharide capsule does not apply. Incorrect Options: A. Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) – Possesses a polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP) polysaccharide capsule, which is a major virulence factor and the target of Hib vaccines. B. Pneumococcus (Streptococcus pneumoniae) – Has a thick polysaccharide capsule, critical for evading phagocytosis and a key vaccine target. C. Neisseria meningitidis – Encapsulated with polysaccharides, with the capsule being essential for virulence and included in meningococcal vaccines.

questions.stem: Among the following, which need only female pathogen and undergo self-fertilization (Parthenogenesis) seen in
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Strongyloides Strongyloides stercoralis has a unique life cycle among intestinal nematodes. It exhibits parthenogenesis, meaning the female worms can reproduce without males in the host. Only female worms are parasitic in humans, and they produce eggs that hatch into larvae capable of continuing the life cycle. This self-fertilization allows Strongyloides to maintain infection in the host even in the absence of male worms. Incorrect Options: A. Trichuris (whipworm) – Requires both male and female worms to reproduce; does not undergo parthenogenesis. C. Ancylostoma (hookworm) – Requires male and female worms for reproduction; parthenogenesis is not seen. D. Enterobius (pinworm) – Male and female worms are both required; reproduction is sexual, not parthenogenetic.

questions.stemHtml: Which option is correct ?

options.label: D
options.text: Prophylaxis given when CD4 count falls 900

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) The statement that Cryptococcus neoformans most commonly causes respiratory infection is TRUE. Infection occurs via inhalation of the encapsulated yeast cells (or spores) from the environment (often associated with pigeon droppings). The primary infection site is the lungs, which may be asymptomatic or present as a mild flu-like illness or pneumonia. However, its most feared manifestation, particularly in immunocompromised patients (like those with HIV/AIDS), is dissemination to the central nervous system, causing meningoencephalitis. The initial, and thus most common, site of infection is still the respiratory tract. Incorrect Options • B. Broad budding cells with pseudohyphae: This is FALSE. Cryptococcus neoformans is a true yeast that reproduces by narrow-based budding and does not form pseudohyphae. The term "broad-based budding" is characteristic of Blastomyces dermatitidis. • C. Human is the only reservoir: This is FALSE. C. neoformans is found widely in the environment (soil, trees) and is heavily associated with pigeon droppings. Humans are accidental hosts infected from the environment; there is no human-to-human transmission. • D. Prophylaxis given when CD4 count falls 900: This is FALSE. Prophylaxis against Cryptococcus is generally not recommended for HIV patients in most settings. If an HIV patient has a CD4 count below 100 cells/?L and is living in an area with high cryptococcal antigen prevalence, some guidelines may consider primary prophylaxis, but 900 cells/?L is a count indicative of a healthy immune system, where prophylaxis is never indicated.

questions.stem: Streptococcus agalactiae causes
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus, GBS) is a major cause of neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis. It colonizes the maternal genital tract and can be transmitted to the newborn during vaginal delivery, leading to early-onset neonatal infection. GBS sepsis is life-threatening and a key reason for maternal screening and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Incorrect Options: A. Infective endocarditis – This is more commonly caused by Streptococcus viridans, Staphylococcus aureus, or Enterococcus, not GBS. B. Dental caries – Caused primarily by Streptococcus mutans, which produces acid that demineralizes teeth. C. Tonsillitis and pharyngitis – Most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus). GBS rarely causes pharyngitis.

questions.stem: Swollen Bartholin opening, vaginal discharge, Clinical picture of PID, Gram negative intra cellular diplococci
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) The combination of the clinical findings and the specific microscopic results points definitively to a gonococcal infection: 1. Gram-negative intracellular diplococci: This is the pathognomonic finding for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, particularly in a specimen from the cervix or urethra. The bacteria are seen as kidney-bean-shaped diplococci located inside polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs). 2. Swollen Bartholin opening (Bartholinitis): Gonorrhea is a very common cause of infection and abscess formation in the Bartholin's glands, whose duct openings are near the vaginal introitus. 3. Vaginal discharge & Clinical picture of PID (Pelvic Inflammatory Disease): N. gonorrhoeae is a major cause of cervicitis, which can ascend to the upper genital tract (uterus, fallopian tubes) to cause PID. Incorrect Options • B. Chlamydia trachomatis: This is a common cause of PID and discharge, but it is an obligate intracellular bacterium that is too small to be seen as distinct diplococci on a Gram stain and requires NAAT or cell culture for diagnosis. • C. Hemophilus ducreyi: This causes chancroid (a painful genital ulcer). It does not cause PID or Barholinitis and is not typically described as intracellular diplococci. • D. Treponema pallidum: This causes Syphilis (painless chancre). This spirochete is not visible on a Gram stain and requires darkfield microscopy or serology for diagnosis.

questions.stemHtml: Patient suffering from diarrhoea. Stool microscopy shown in the image measures 15 -20 microns oocyst. Identify the structure
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Cystoisospora belli The image shows a large, oval (ellipsoidal) oocyst containing two internal sporoblasts (the two large purple structures). The prompt states the oocyst measures 15-20 ?m, which is within the characteristic size range for Cystoisospora belli (formerly Isospora belli), typically measuring 20 to 30 ?m in length. This protozoan causes cystoisosporiasis, a diarrheal illness. The key diagnostic features visible are its large size, elliptical shape, and the presence of internal sporocysts/sporoblasts (often two when passed in stool, which then mature outside the host). Incorrect Options • B. Cyclospora: The oocysts of Cyclospora cayetanensis are distinctly smaller and spherical, measuring 8?10 ?m. • C. Cryptosporidium: The oocysts of Cryptosporidium parvum are the smallest of these coccidial parasites, measuring 4?6 ?m and are spherical. • D. Microsporidia: These are a group of spore-forming fungi. Their spores are minute (1?4 ?m), much smaller than the structure shown, and require specialized stains for visualization.

questions.stem: Best diagnostic test for malaria speciation
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Giemsa-stained thin smear The Giemsa-stained thin smear is the best test for malaria speciation. While the thick smear is more sensitive for detecting parasitemia, it does not preserve the morphology of red blood cells well, making it difficult to identify the Plasmodium species. The thin smear, in contrast, allows clear visualization of the parasite inside RBCs, enabling differentiation between P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, and P. ovale based on size, shape, and arrangement within RBCs. Incorrect Options: A. Giemsa-stained thick smear – Highly sensitive for detecting the presence of malaria parasites, but not ideal for species identification because RBC morphology is lost. C. Acridine orange-stained thin slide – Useful for rapid detection of malaria parasites under fluorescence microscopy, but does not allow reliable species identification. D. Calcofluor white – Stains fungal cell walls, not malaria parasites, and is irrelevant for malaria diagnosis.

questions.stem: Extensive h/o Dengue hemorrhagic fever , retro orbital pain - H/ 0 fever for more than 5 days presentation - Best test for diagnosis
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) IgM Capture ELISA In a patient with fever for more than 5 days and a history of dengue hemorrhagic fever, the acute viremic phase has usually passed, so NS1 antigen and RT-PCR are no longer reliable. At this stage, the body has started producing IgM antibodies, which are detectable by IgM capture ELISA. This makes IgM ELISA the best diagnostic test for dengue in the late acute or early convalescent phase (typically after day 5 of illness). Incorrect Options: A. NS1 antigen – Detectable only during the first 1–5 days of infection; not useful after day 5. C. RT-PCR – Detects viral RNA in the early viremic phase (first 5 days); after this period, RNA levels drop, making the test less reliable. D. Albopictus mosquito cell culture – Rarely used clinically due to complexity and slow turnaround; also mainly useful for research rather than routine diagnosis.

questions.stem: PARVO B19 does not cause
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Aplastic anaemia in immunocompromised Parvovirus B19 primarily infects erythroid precursor cells, leading to temporary cessation of red cell production. This can cause transient aplastic anemia, especially in patients with underlying hemolytic disorders. In pregnant women, infection can lead to non-immune hydrops fetalis due to fetal anemia. It can also cause fever with a characteristic “slapped cheek” rash in children (erythema infectiosum). However, Parvovirus B19 is not a typical cause of chronic or persistent aplastic anemia in immunocompromised patients; other causes like chemotherapy, autoimmune disorders, or other viral infections (e.g., EBV, HIV) are responsible. Incorrect Options: A. Transient aplastic anemia – Classic complication in individuals with increased red cell turnover or hemolytic anemia; well-documented. C. Non-immune hydrops fetalis – Occurs due to fetal anemia from Parvovirus B19 infection during pregnancy. D. Fever with petechial rash – Common manifestation in children and adults; the rash is often accompanied by mild febrile illness.

questions.stem: Which organism transmitted through all blood components
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum, is transmitted through all blood components, including plasma, platelets, and red cells. The spirochete can survive in stored blood for a limited time and thus poses a risk in transfusion-transmitted infections. This is why blood donors are routinely screened for syphilis to prevent transmission. A. Malaria – Transmitted only through red cell transfusions, as the parasite (Plasmodium) resides inside erythrocytes. It is not present in all components like plasma or platelets. B. Filaria – Wuchereria bancrofti and related species are transmitted via mosquito vectors, not blood transfusion. Microfilariae do not survive well in stored blood. C. Toxoplasma – Can be transmitted through organ transplantation or rarely through blood transfusion, but not through all components. Risk is mainly from leukocytes.

questions.stem: How to disinfect disposable mouth piece of glass pipette A. Autoclave B. Hot air oven C. Ethanol 70% D.Microwave
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) A, B are Correct A. Autoclave: This is the most effective method for sterilizing glass pipettes. Autoclaving uses high pressure and temperature (typically 121°C) to kill all microorganisms, including resistant spores. Glass is heat-resistant and can easily withstand the autoclaving process, making it ideal for sterilization. B. Hot air oven: This is also a valid method for sterilizing glass pipettes. It uses dry heat, typically at 160°C to 180°C, to sterilize glass. This method is effective but generally takes longer than autoclaving. C. Ethanol 70%: Ethanol can be used for disinfection, but it doesn't achieve sterilization. While it can reduce the microbial load on the glass surface, it doesn't kill all forms of bacteria or viruses, especially more resistant organisms like spores. D. Microwave: This is not a suitable method for sterilizing glass pipettes. Microwaving could lead to uneven heating and may not be effective in killing microorganisms. Glass pipettes may also get damaged in the microwave.

questions.stem: Mother with H/o painful genital lesions one year bedore. 18 days old Child has CNS symptoms and multinucleated giant cells seen. Cause is
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection is most often caused by HSV-2, which is transmitted perinatally from mothers with genital herpes, even if the infection occurred in the past. In neonates, HSV-2 commonly causes CNS involvement (encephalitis, seizures, lethargy), disseminated infection, or localized skin, eye, and mouth disease. The presence of multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear is characteristic of herpesvirus infections (HSV and VZV). Since the mother had painful genital lesions previously and the neonate now shows CNS disease with giant cells, HSV-2 is the most likely cause. Incorrect Options: A. VZV (Varicella zoster virus) – Also produces multinucleated giant cells but usually causes congenital varicella syndrome (limb hypoplasia, cicatricial skin lesions) or neonatal varicella, not isolated neonatal CNS disease following maternal genital lesions. C. Coxsackie virus – Can cause neonatal myocarditis, meningitis, or sepsis-like illness, but does not produce multinucleated giant cells on smear. D. Haemophilus ducreyi – Causes chancroid (painful genital ulcers) in adults, not neonatal CNS infection, and does not produce giant cells.

questions.stemHtml: A farmer came with nodular lesions along with lymphatic drainage. Microscopy shown here. Choose the correct pathogen.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Sporothrix The clinical presentation of a patient (a farmer) with nodular lesions along lymphatic drainage is the classic description of lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis (often called "rose gardener's disease"). 1. Clinical Correlation: The sporotrichoid pattern is caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a dimorphic fungus found in soil, plants, and decaying wood. Traumatic inoculation (e.g., from a rose thorn or splinter) leads to a primary lesion followed by a chain of secondary nodules tracking along the lymphatic channels. 2. Microscopy: The image shows the mold form of the fungus, characterized by slender, branching hyphae bearing small, tear-drop or pear-shaped conidia in clusters at the tips of the conidiophores. This arrangement is classically described as a "rosette" or "daisy-head" pattern, which is the definitive appearance of the Sporothrix mold form grown in culture at 25?C. Incorrect Options • B. Histoplasma: This dimorphic fungus causes histoplasmosis. Its mold form produces two types of spores: microconidia and large, spiked tuberculate macroconidia, which do not match the image. • C. Blastomyces: This dimorphic fungus causes blastomycosis. Its mold form produces small, pear-shaped conidia directly on hyphal branches, giving it a lollypop appearance, which is different from the rosette pattern shown. • D. Coccidioides: This dimorphic fungus causes coccidioidomycosis. Its mold form is characterized by barrel-shaped arthroconidia alternating with empty cells, which is completely different from the morphology shown.

questions.stem: Choose the water borne hepatitis virus
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is a picornavirus transmitted primarily via the fecal–oral route, often through contaminated water or food. It is the classic water-borne hepatitis virus and commonly causes outbreaks in areas with poor sanitation. The infection is usually self-limiting, does not cause chronic hepatitis, and has an excellent prognosis. Incorrect Options: B. HBV (Hepatitis B virus) – Transmitted by blood, sexual contact, and perinatally from mother to child. Not water-borne. C. HCV (Hepatitis C virus) – Spread mainly through blood transfusion, intravenous drug abuse, and unsafe injections. No water transmission. D. HDV (Hepatitis D virus) – A defective virus that requires HBV coinfection for replication; transmitted through blood and body fluids, not via water.

questions.stem: Medium for M. tuberculosis
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) LJ medium Lowenstein–Jensen (LJ) medium is the standard medium used for the culture of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is an egg-based medium that contains malachite green, which inhibits the growth of contaminating bacteria, while supporting the slow growth of M. tuberculosis. Colonies typically appear as rough, tough, and buff (RTB) after 4–6 weeks. This is the gold standard for TB culture and drug susceptibility testing. Incorrect Options: B. SDA (Sabouraud’s Dextrose Agar) – Specialized medium used for culturing fungi, not M. tuberculosis. C. Muller Hinton agar – Used mainly for antibiotic susceptibility testing (e.g., Kirby–Bauer disk diffusion), not for TB culture. D. Blood agar – Supports the growth of many fastidious bacteria, such as Streptococcus and Staphylococcus, but not suitable for slow-growing mycobacteria.

questions.stem: A patient came with blunt injury from farm instrument in chest. Pus from wound shows Gram positive filamentous bacteria which is partially acid fast. Choose the correct pathogen.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Nocardia Nocardia species are aerobic, Gram-positive filamentous bacteria that are partially acid-fast due to the presence of mycolic acids in their cell wall. They are commonly found in soil and decaying organic matter, which explains the association with farm-related injuries or trauma involving soil contamination. Clinically, Nocardia can cause cutaneous infections, particularly wounds contaminated with soil, and may also lead to systemic infections in immunocompromised patients. The combination of Gram-positive filamentous appearance and partial acid-fastness is highly characteristic of Nocardia, making it the correct pathogen in this scenario. Incorrect Options: A. Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) Anthrax is a Gram-positive spore-forming rod, not filamentous, and is non–acid fast. Cutaneous anthrax presents as a painless ulcer with a black eschar, not typically with pus showing filamentous bacteria. B. Listeria (Listeria monocytogenes) Listeria is a small Gram-positive rod, non-filamentous, and non–acid fast. It mainly causes neonatal infections, sepsis, and meningitis, not soil-related wound infections. C. Diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) Corynebacterium is Gram-positive and club-shaped, non-filamentous, and non–acid fast. It causes respiratory diphtheria or cutaneous ulcers, but not the filamentous, partially acid-fast appearance seen in Nocardia.

questions.stem: Which is not a cold sterilization
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Autoclave Autoclaving is not a cold sterilization method because it relies on moist heat under pressure (typically 121°C at 15 psi for 15–20 minutes) to kill microorganisms. The high temperature denatures proteins and destroys microbial structures, which classifies it as heat sterilization, not cold sterilization. Cold sterilization methods, in contrast, sterilize without using high temperatures. Incorrect Options: A. Gamma radiation Gamma radiation is a cold sterilization method that uses ionizing radiation to disrupt DNA of microorganisms, effectively sterilizing materials like medical equipment and pharmaceuticals without heat. B. UV rays Ultraviolet (UV) radiation is a cold sterilization method that kills microorganisms by causing thymine dimers in DNA, used for sterilizing surfaces and air. D. Gas Plasma sterilization Gas plasma sterilization (e.g., hydrogen peroxide plasma) is a low-temperature sterilization technique, making it a form of cold sterilization, suitable for heat-sensitive instruments.

questions.stem: DOC for Fasciola hepatica
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Triclabendazole: Triclabendazole is the drug of choice for Fasciola hepatica infection because it is highly effective against both the immature and adult stages of the parasite. It works by inhibiting the parasite’s tubulin function, leading to paralysis and death of the fluke. A single or two-dose regimen is usually sufficient for complete cure, making it the preferred treatment. Incorrect Options: A – Albendazole: Albendazole has some activity against Fasciola hepatica, but it is less effective compared to triclabendazole and usually requires prolonged therapy. It is not the first-line choice. C – Mebendazole: Mebendazole is mainly effective against intestinal nematodes and has minimal or unreliable activity against liver flukes. It is not recommended for Fasciola infections. D – Praziquantel: Praziquantel is highly effective against many trematodes and cestodes, but it has poor efficacy against Fasciola hepatica. Therefore, it is not used for treatment of fascioliasis.

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Rectal prolapse is not a feature of Ascaris lumbricoides infection. This parasite primarily resides in the small intestine, and while it can cause intestinal obstruction, malnutrition, or biliary/pancreatic complications, it does not typically cause rectal prolapse. Incorrect Options: B – Asthma-like symptoms: Ascaris larvae migrate through the lungs during their life cycle (Löffler’s syndrome), which can produce cough, wheezing, and transient asthma-like symptoms. C – Unembryonated egg takes time for fertilization: Ascaris eggs are initially unembryonated when passed in stool and require a few weeks in the external environment to develop into infective embryonated eggs, which is accurate. D – Mostly asymptomatic: Most Ascaris infections, especially in light infections, are asymptomatic. Symptoms usually appear only in heavy infestations.

questions.stem: The following one is antibiotic sensitivity testing.
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer (D)

E test

An E test, or Epsilometer test, is a method used in microbiology to determine the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of an antibiotic. A strip with a gradient of antibiotic concentration is placed on an agar plate inoculated with bacteria. The MIC is determined by the point where the elliptical zone of inhibition intersects the strip, indicating the lowest concentration of the antibiotic that prevents visible bacterial growth. This method is a form of antibiotic sensitivity testing.

questions.stem: True statements about Cryptococcus A. Extra pulmonary is aids defining illness B. Reservoir for C.gatti is Bird C. All pathogenic species are urease +ve D. Commonly seen in CD4500
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) A, B, C: • Cryptococcus infection outside the lungs (extra-pulmonary), especially meningoencephalitis, is an AIDS-defining illness. • C. gattii commonly has a reservoir in trees (especially eucalyptus), while C. neoformans is associated with bird droppings. The statement refers to environmental reservoirs; the bird association is primarily for C. neoformans. • All pathogenic species of Cryptococcus are urease positive, which is an important virulence factor facilitating survival in the host. Incorrect Options: B – A and D: Incorrect because Cryptococcus infection is most common in immunocompromised individuals with CD4 <100>500. C – B and D: Incorrect for the same reason as above; CD4 >500 is not commonly associated with disease. D – C and D: Again incorrect because while urease positivity is true, disease is uncommon in patients with CD4 >500.

questions.stem: Wire loop is sterilized by
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Heat till become red A wire loop used in microbiology for streaking cultures must be sterilized by direct flaming until it becomes red hot. This method ensures complete destruction of microbial contaminants, including spores, and is quick and effective for tools that can withstand high temperatures. Incorrect Options: A – Autoclave: Autoclaving is used for sterilizing heat-resistant lab glassware, media, and instruments, but it is not practical for a small wire loop that needs rapid sterilization between streaks. B – Microwaved: Microwaving does not reliably sterilize a wire loop, as it cannot uniformly reach the temperatures required to kill all microorganisms and spores. D – Gamma rays: Gamma radiation is used for sterilizing disposable medical equipment and pharmaceuticals, not for immediate sterilization of lab tools like wire loops.
