questions.stem: Rapid spread of Necrotizing fasciitis in previously injured skin shows Gram positive cocci in chains. Choose the correct pathogen.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Strep. pyogenes S. pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) is the most common cause of rapidly spreading necrotizing fasciitis. It presents as Gram-positive cocci in chains on Gram stain and can invade soft tissue following minor trauma, causing severe pain, edema, and systemic toxicity. Its virulence is due to exotoxins and enzymes that rapidly destroy fascia and subcutaneous tissue. Incorrect Options: B – Staphylococcus aureus: S. aureus is a Gram-positive cocci in clusters and usually causes localized abscesses rather than rapidly spreading necrotizing fasciitis. Methicillin-resistant strains (MRSA) can complicate infections but are less commonly associated with classical necrotizing fasciitis. C – Clostridium perfringens: This is a Gram-positive, spore-forming bacillus causing gas gangrene (myonecrosis), not the typical rapidly spreading necrotizing fasciitis seen with Gram-positive cocci in chains. D – Vibrio vulnificus: This Gram-negative rod causes necrotizing soft tissue infections, usually in seawater-exposed wounds or in immunocompromised patients, but it is not the classic pathogen for post-traumatic necrotizing fasciitis with Gram-positive cocci.

questions.stem: Which is not a passive immunity
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Toxoids are inactivated bacterial toxins used as vaccines (e.g., diphtheria or tetanus toxoid) to stimulate the body’s own immune system to produce antibodies. This generates active immunity, not passive immunity, because protection is achieved by the host’s own immune response over time. Incorrect Options: A – Antitoxin: Antitoxins are preformed antibodies given to a person to neutralize toxins immediately, providing passive immunity. B – Monoclonal antibody: Monoclonal antibodies are laboratory-produced antibodies administered for immediate protection or therapy, representing passive immunity. C – IgA: Maternal IgA in breast milk provides passive immunity to the infant by protecting mucosal surfaces without requiring the infant to generate its own immune response.

questions.stemHtml: Single cyst in right hepatic area. Liver aspirate shown in the image. Choose the correct pathogen.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) The image shows microscopic structures recovered from a single cyst in the hepatic area (liver). The structure is a hydatid cyst wall with key diagnostic components highlighted: 1. Brood Capsule: The image shows a larger, thin-walled, circular structure (indicated by the red arrow/outline) that buds internally from the germinal layer of the hydatid cyst. 2. Protoscolex: Inside the brood capsule, there are smaller structures (one circled in red, one indicated by a small red circle) that are protoscolices. These are the tapeworm heads that will mature into adult tapeworms if ingested by a definitive host (like a dog). They are identifiable by their characteristic hooklets and suckers. The presence of a single hepatic cyst containing protoscolices and brood capsules is pathognomonic for Cystic Echinococcosis (Hydatid Disease), caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. Incorrect Options • A. Taenia: This genus of tapeworms (e.g., T. solium, T. saginata) causes Taeniasis (adult worms in the intestine). While T. solium can cause Cysticercosis (larval cysts in tissue), the cysts contain only a single, fully developed cysticercus, not brood capsules and multiple protoscolices as seen in a hydatid cyst. • B. H. Nana (Hymenolepis nana): This tapeworm causes Hymenolepiasis. It does not form large, fluid-filled cysts in organs like the liver. Its diagnosis is based on finding characteristic eggs in stool. • D. Latum (Diphyllobothrium latum): This is the Broad Fish Tapeworm. It resides only in the human intestine as an adult worm and does not cause larval cysts in the liver.

questions.stem: Common cause of diarrhoea and dehydration in children is
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Rota virus Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe gastroenteritis, diarrhea, and dehydration in children under 5 years of age worldwide. It infects the enterocytes of the small intestine, leading to malabsorption, watery diarrhea, vomiting, and fever. Rotavirus infection can be prevented by vaccination. Incorrect Options: A – Norwalk virus: Also known as norovirus, it primarily causes acute gastroenteritis outbreaks in older children and adults, not the most common cause in young children. C – Shigella: Shigella causes dysentery with bloody diarrhea and is less commonly associated with severe dehydration compared to rotavirus in children. D – Enterobius: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) primarily causes perianal itching, not diarrhoea or dehydration.

questions.stem: All the following are COVID 19 preventive measures except
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Ivermectin prophylaxis Ivermectin is an antiparasitic drug that has not been proven effective for the prevention of COVID-19. Its use as a prophylactic measure is not recommended by WHO, CDC, or national guidelines. Incorrect Options: A – Wearing mask: Masking reduces the risk of SARS-CoV-2 transmission by preventing respiratory droplet spread. B – Vaccination: COVID-19 vaccines are a primary preventive measure, reducing both infection risk and severity of disease. C – Cough etiquette: Proper cough and sneeze hygiene prevents the spread of respiratory droplets, which is an established infection control practice.

questions.stem: A child admitted with haematuria, thrombocytopenia and Bloody diarrhoea. Choose the correct pathogen
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC), especially the O157:H7 serotype, is the most common cause of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) in children. It produces Shiga toxin, leading to endothelial damage, resulting in bloody diarrhoea, hematuria, and thrombocytopenia. This is a classic post-diarrheal complication in pediatric patients. Incorrect Options: A – Salmonella: Causes gastroenteritis or enteric fever but is rarely associated with HUS. C – Yersinia: Typically causes enterocolitis, mesenteric lymphadenitis, or reactive arthritis; it is not a common cause of HUS. D – E. coli: While generic E. coli can cause diarrhea, only enterohemorrhagic strains like O157:H7 are associated with HUS and bloody diarrhea.

questions.answerText: Inhibits the release of GABA and GLYCINE
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Tetanus toxin (Clostridium tetani) is a neurotoxin that blocks inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine in the central nervous system. This results in unopposed excitatory signals, leading to characteristic muscle rigidity and spasms such as lockjaw (trismus) and opisthotonus. Incorrect Options: A – Inhibits acetylcholine: Incorrect. Tetanus does not inhibit acetylcholine release; instead, acetylcholine release continues unchecked at neuromuscular junctions due to loss of inhibitory control. C – Inhibits protein synthesis: This is the mechanism of diphtheria toxin, not tetanus toxin. D – Inhibits cAMP cage: This is the mechanism of cholera toxin, which increases cAMP leading to watery diarrhea, not tetanus.

questions.stemHtml: Child with anal Pruritis, Microscopy of the pathogen shown here. Choose the correct pathogen..
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) The clinical presentation of a child with anal pruritis (perianal itching) is the classic sign of Enterobiasis (Pinworm infection). The microscopy image confirms this diagnosis by showing the characteristic egg of Enterobius vermicularis: 1. Morphology: The egg is typically oval/ellipsoidal and distinctly asymmetrical (plano-convex), meaning one side is flattened and the other is curved. 2. Contents: It contains a developing larva (or a fully developed one). 3. Diagnosis: Pinworm infection is diagnosed by the "Scotch tape test" (or perianal swab) because the female worm lays her eggs in the perianal folds at night, leading to the severe itching (pruritis) that disrupts the child's sleep. Incorrect Options • A. Trichuris (Whipworm): The egg of Trichuris trichiura is distinctly barrel-shaped with clear, prominent bipolar plugs, a morphology completely different from the egg shown. • C. Ascaris (Roundworm): The eggs of Ascaris lumbricoides are typically oval, thick-shelled, and have a bumpy, albuminous outer coat (corticated) or a smooth, thick shell (decorticated). They are not asymmetrical. • D. Ancylostoma (Hookworm): Hookworm eggs are thin-shelled, oval, and contain a cleaving embryo (2-8 blastomeres) when fresh, which is also clearly different from the asymmetrical egg shown.

Blotting techniques are essential molecular biology tools used to transfer separated macromolecules (DNA, RNA, or protein) from a gel to a solid support membrane, where they can be detected using specific probes.

questions.stem: PLHIV presented with dysphagia and odynophagia. White plaques observed in upper GI endoscope. Biopsy image may reveal
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) In PLHIV (immunocompromised patients), esophageal candidiasis is a common cause of dysphagia and odynophagia. Biopsy typically shows yeast cells with pseudohyphae of Candida species invading the mucosa. White plaques on endoscopy are characteristic. Incorrect Options: A – Multinucleated giant cell: Seen in viral infections like herpes simplex virus (HSV) or cytomegalovirus (CMV), not typical for candidiasis. B – Aseptate hyphae: Aseptate hyphae are characteristic of Mucorales (mucormycosis), which usually presents with tissue necrosis rather than white esophageal plaques. D – Acid-fast bacteria: Acid-fast bacilli indicate Mycobacterium infection (e.g., TB), which does not present with white plaques in the esophagus.

questions.stem: Choose the autoinfection causing Parasite
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) S. stercoralis has a unique autoinfection cycle, where rhabditiform larvae can mature into infective filariform larvae within the host and re-infect the intestinal mucosa or perianal skin. This can lead to chronic, persistent infection, sometimes lasting decades, and in immunocompromised patients, it may cause hyperinfection syndrome. Incorrect Options: B – Ancylostoma duodenale: Hookworms do not cause autoinfection; infection occurs via skin penetration by filariform larvae from contaminated soil. C – Ascaris lumbricoides: Infection occurs via ingestion of embryonated eggs; no autoinfection occurs. D – Hymenolepis nana: Although H. nana can occasionally show internal autoinfection in humans, autoinfection is rare, and S. stercoralis is the classic parasite known for autoinfection.

questions.stem: All the following are Dimorphic Fungi except
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Cryptococcus species are not dimorphic fungi; they exist primarily as yeasts in the environment and in human tissue. Dimorphic fungi, in contrast, can exist as mold in the environment and yeast or spherule in human tissue. Incorrect Options: A – Coccidioides: Dimorphic fungus; exists as arthroconidia in soil and spherules in tissue. B – Talaromyces (formerly Penicillium marneffei): Dimorphic fungus; mold at 25°C and yeast at 37°C. C – Histoplasma: Dimorphic fungus; mycelial form in environment and yeast form in tissue.

questions.stem: Treatment option for penicillin resistant gonococcal infection is
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin, is the drug of choice for penicillin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It is highly effective against most strains and is recommended as a single intramuscular dose for uncomplicated gonococcal infections. Incorrect Options: A – Vancomycin: Vancomycin is primarily active against Gram-positive bacteria and has no role in treating gonococcal infections. B – Tetracycline: Tetracycline resistance is common in N. gonorrhoeae, so it is not recommended as first-line therapy. D – Amoxicillin: Many gonococcal strains are resistant to penicillin and amoxicillin, making this drug ineffective for penicillin-resistant infections.

questions.stemHtml: Choose the organism identified by the method shown in the image
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) The image demonstrates the phenomenon of satellitism, a key identification test for Haemophilus influenzae. 1. Satellitism: This describes the characteristic growth pattern where small, fastidious bacteria grow only in the enhanced nutrient zone surrounding colonies of certain other bacteria. 2. Mechanism: Haemophilus influenzae requires two factors for growth: o X factor (Hemin): A heat-stable component of hemoglobin. o V factor (NAD/Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide): A heat-labile coenzyme. 3. Plate Setup: The image shows H. influenzae being inoculated across a Blood Agar plate, followed by a streak of S. aureus (labeled S. aureus). 4. Result: S. aureus colonies produce and secrete the V factor (NAD) into the agar, and their beta-hemolysis releases the X factor (Hemin) from the red blood cells. H. influenzae colonies, therefore, grow best (like satellites) only in the rich zone immediately surrounding the S. aureus streak, confirming the identity of the tiny colonies as H. influenzae. Incorrect Options • A. Streptococcus pneumoniae: This bacterium is typically identified by its alpha-hemolysis and Optochin sensitivity, not satellitism. • C. Corynebacterium diphtheriae: This is a Gram-positive rod identified by its characteristic Chinese letter arrangement on Gram stain and toxin production, not by satellitism. • D. Klebsiella pneumoniae: This is a large, non-fastidious Gram-negative rod that grows as very mucoid colonies on standard agar media without requiring helper organisms.

questions.stem: Choose the bacteria exhibits Kanagawa phenomenon in Wagatsuma agar
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) V. parahaemolyticus produces thermostable direct hemolysin (TDH), which causes the Kanagawa phenomenon—beta-hemolysis on Wagatsuma agar containing human red blood cells. This hemolytic activity is used as a marker of pathogenic strains. Incorrect Options: A – Burkholderia mallei: Causes glanders; does not exhibit Kanagawa phenomenon. B – Vibrio cholerae: Causes cholera; does not produce hemolysis on Wagatsuma agar. D – Staphylococcus aureus: Produces hemolysins on blood agar, but Kanagawa phenomenon is specific to V. parahaemolyticus on Wagatsuma agar.

questions.stem: All the following are High risk group for HIV except
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Truck drivers are not inherently a high-risk group for HIV. While some may engage in high-risk behaviors such as unprotected sex or visiting sex workers, being a truck driver alone does not classify them as a high-risk group. Incorrect Options: A – MSM: Men who have sex with men are at high risk due to higher rates of HIV transmission through receptive anal intercourse. B – IDU: Intravenous drug users are at high risk because sharing needles can transmit HIV directly into the bloodstream. D – CSW: Commercial sex workers are considered high risk due to frequent exposure to multiple sexual partners, increasing the probability of HIV transmission.

Correct Answer (C)

The correct match for the arthropod vectors and the rickettsial diseases they transmit is C. a-3, b-2, c-4, d-1.
Detailed Rationale
• Louse (a?3): The body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis) is the primary vector for Epidemic Typhus (R. prowazekii).
• Tick (b?2): Various species of ticks (e.g., Dermacentor) transmit Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF) (R. rickettsii).
• Rat Flea (c?4): The rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis) is the vector that transmits Endemic (Murine) Typhus (R. typhi) from rodents to humans.
• Mite (d?1): The house mouse mite (Liponyssoides sanguineus) is the vector for Rickettsial Pox (R. akari). (Note: Scrub typhus is also transmitted by mites, but Rickettsial Pox is the correct match among the choices)

questions.stem: Choose the correct statement(s) 1. Weil Felix test for typhus fever 2. Widal test done in first week of fever h& wRk 3. Standard agglutination test for brucellosis SAT 4. Microscopic agglutination test for Leptospirosis
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) • Weil-Felix test is a classic serological test for typhus fever, based on cross-reactivity with Proteus OX antigens. • SAT (Standard Agglutination Test) is used for brucellosis to detect antibodies in patient serum. • MAT (Microscopic Agglutination Test) is the gold standard for leptospirosis. Incorrect Options: 2 – Widal test in first week of fever: Widal test is not reliable in the first week of typhoid fever because antibodies (O and H) develop after 7–10 days. Testing too early may yield false negatives, so statement 2 is incorrect. Other combinations: Any option including statement 2 is incorrect because of the early timing limitation of Widal test.

questions.stem: Most common HPV serotypes associated with human cervical cancer is
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Human papillomavirus (HPV) types 16 and 18 are the most oncogenic and are responsible for approximately 70% of cervical cancers worldwide. These are considered high-risk HPV types. Incorrect Options: A – 31, 33: Also high-risk types, but less common than 16 and 18 in cervical cancer. C – 6, 11: Low-risk HPV types; associated with genital warts and benign lesions, not cervical cancer. D – 1, 4: Cause cutaneous warts (plantar or common warts), not associated with cervical cancer

questions.stem: Patient with painful vesicular genital lesion, DOC is
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Painful vesicular genital lesions are most commonly caused by Herpes simplex virus (HSV-2). Acyclovir, an antiviral drug, is the drug of choice for both treatment and suppression of HSV infections. It inhibits viral DNA polymerase, limiting viral replication and reducing symptom severity. Incorrect Options: A – Penicillin: Effective against syphilis (Treponema pallidum), which usually causes painless ulcer (chancre), not painful vesicles. C – Ceftriaxone: Used for gonococcal infections, which may present as urethral discharge, not vesicular genital lesions. D – Erythromycin: Macrolide antibiotic; not effective against viral infections like HSV.

questions.stemHtml: An adult male patient with the H/o unprotected sex few months ago presented with the clinical feature shown in the image. Choose the ideal laboratory test to diagnose this condition.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) The clinical presentation is a textbook case of Secondary Syphilis, caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. The primary chancre has usually healed by this stage, and the body's immune system has mounted a significant response. • Rationale: The diagnosis of secondary syphilis is almost always confirmed using serological tests which detect antibodies produced by the body against T. pallidum. These include: o Non-treponemal tests (screening): VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) or RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin). These measure antibodies against cardiolipin-lecithin-cholesterol antigen (reagin). o Treponemal tests (confirmatory): TP-PA (T. pallidum Particle Agglutination) or FTA-ABS (Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption). These measure antibodies specific to the T. pallidum organism. • By the secondary stage, both non-treponemal and treponemal tests are typically highly positive (reactive). Incorrect Options • A. Tzanck smear: This test is used to detect multinucleated giant cells and inclusion bodies, which are characteristic of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) or Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) infections (vesicular lesions). It is not used for syphilis. • B. KOH wet mount: This is used to dissolve keratin and visualize fungal elements (hyphae and spores) to diagnose conditions like tinea or candidiasis. It is not relevant for syphilis. • D. Skin biopsy: A skin biopsy may show characteristic inflammatory infiltrates, but it is invasive and generally considered a supportive or last-resort test. The diagnosis is routinely and reliably established using non-invasive serology.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the Immunoglobulin structure shown in the image
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) The structure shown is a dimer (two Y-shaped immunoglobulin monomers joined together) and features a central component that links the two monomers. This is the characteristic structure of Secretory IgA (SIgA). 1. Dimerization: The structure consists of two Ig monomers (two Y-shaped units, each composed of two heavy and two light chains). 2. J Chain: The two monomers are linked together by a small, central polypeptide called the J (Joining) chain (represented by the purple structure in the center). 3. Secretory Component: While not explicitly detailed, in its secreted form (which this structure often represents), it would also include a secretory component wrapped around the dimer. Incorrect Options • A. IgM: This immunoglobulin exists as a pentamer (five Y-shaped units) in serum, forming a large, wheel-like structure, linked by a J chain. • B. IgE: This is typically a monomer (a single Y-shaped unit). • C. IgG: This is the most abundant immunoglobulin and exists primarily as a monomer (a single Y-shaped unit).

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Enterovirus 70 is the primary cause of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis, a highly contagious eye infection characterized by sudden onset of redness, swelling, and subconjunctival hemorrhage. Transmission is typically via direct contact or contaminated fomites. Incorrect Options: B – Coxsackie A: May cause hand-foot-mouth disease and herpangina, but not typically associated with hemorrhagic conjunctivitis. C – Coxsackie B: Mainly causes myocarditis, pericarditis, and systemic infections, not ocular hemorrhagic disease. D – Enterovirus 72: Not commonly associated with hemorrhagic conjunctivitis.
